"""Course Description

This final course in the Master of Data Science program challenges students to apply their data science knowledge to real-world scenarios. Students will engage with provided datasets accompanied by detailed contextual information that simulates authentic business environments and organizational objectives. This capstone experience requires students to synthesize knowledge from their previous coursework while exercising independent problem-solving and critical-thinking skills. The course emphasizes the practical application of data science within relevant social, organizational, and institutional contexts.
Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to: 

- Navigate a complete data science lifecycle from problem formulation to solution delivery by applying standardized methodologies to real-world business scenarios.

- Develop and implement data-driven solutions that effectively address business objectives within relevant social, organizational, and institutional contexts.

- Apply appropriate data cleaning preparation, modeling, and visualization techniques to derive meaningful insights from complex datasets that address specific organizational needs.

- Communicate findings effectively through professional deliverables tailored to various stakeholder audiences.

- Demonstrate mastery of core data science concepts and skills through the successful completion of end-to-end case studies.

- Document your implementation process and describe your decisions, challenges, and learning throughout the project.
Topical Outline

    Unit 1 - Project Foundation and Data Discovery

        Module 1 - Introduction to the Course and CRISP-DM Framework

        Module 2 - CRISP-DM Phase 1: Business Understanding (Part 1)

        Module 3 - CRISP-DM Phase 1: Business Understanding (Part 2)

        Module 4 - CRISP-DM Phase 2: Data Understanding (Part 1)

        Module 5 - CRISP-DM Phase 2: Data Understanding (Part 2)

    Unit 2 - Data Preparation and Model Development

        Module 6 - CRISP-DM Phase 3: Data Preparation (Part 1)

        Module 7 - CRISP-DM Phase 3: Data Preparation (Part 2)

        Module 8 - CRISP-DM Phase 4: Modeling (Part 1)

        Module 9 - CRISP-DM Phase 4: Modeling (Part 2)

    Unit 3 - Model Assessment and Implementation

        Module 10 - CRISP-DM Phase 5: Evaluation (Part 1)

        Module 11 - CRISP-DM Phase 5: Evaluation (Part 2)

        Module 12 - CRISP-DM Phase 6: Deployment (Part 1)

        Module 13 - CRISP-DM Phase 6: Deployment (Part 2)

        Module 14 - Course Wrap Up and Final Project Synthesis

Required Textbooks

There are no required textbooks for purchase.

Readings will be available as open resources online or through the University Library System. If you encounter any difficulties accessing library reasons, please contact the University Library System through their Ask Us

 form or chat.
Software

This course requires a functioning Python Data Science Environment. Please see the “Setting up your Workspace” reading item for more information.
Graded Assignments

There are three major assignments in this course. These assignments will evaluate your learning at the end of the three major instructional units in the course. They have a higher impact on your final grade, will assess your learning across multiple modules, and will involve more time to complete. Because these assessments have a bigger impact on your grade and require more time, it's important to start preparing well in advance. This might involve remaining up to date with the modules and developing your learning through reading items and quizzes.

    Module 5 - Business and Data Understanding Report

    Module 9 - Data Preparation and Modeling Report

    Module 13 - Final Report

Grading Scheme

All assessments will be submitted electronically on the Coursera site before the conclusion of the course.
Assignment Grade Disputes

An evaluation grade can be appealed up to two weeks after it has been returned. After this point, no appeals will be considered. The goal of a grade appeal is to ensure a fair and consistent score. Thus, a score will not be adjusted on an issue of partial credit if the awarded points are consistent with the grading policy adopted for the class as a whole.

When appealing a grade, contact the instructional team for the course and include a rationale for why you are requesting a re-grade; re-grades are typically acted upon based on possible errors, such as point miscalculation, pieces of assignments that were overlooked, discrepancies between what students were tasked with completing and how they were graded, or late assignments that were penalized even though extenuating circumstances were documented. The instructional team will look for mistakes in the original grading or in the application of grade penalties as well as review documentation of extenuating circumstances if such documentation was not factored into the original grade. The entire assignment will be re-graded by the instructional team, so the score may increase, remain the same, or even decrease. Once the re-grade has occurred, either it will be noted in your grade report for the course or the instructional team will notify you of the outcome of the regrade.
Late Work Policy

Assignment deadlines are set for 11:59 PM Eastern Time (ET). Assignments submitted after the due date/time will be assessed a late penalty of 10% per day. Assignments will not be accepted more than 8 days after the original due date. 

Extension Requests

If you anticipate needing additional time to complete an assignment, please reach out to the instructor before the due date to discuss your situation. Extensions may be granted on a case-by-case basis.
Academic Integrity

Students in this course will be expected to comply with the University of Pittsburgh’s Policy on Academic Integrity

. Any student suspected of violating this obligation for any reason during the semester will be required to participate in the procedural process, initiated at the instructor level, as outlined in the University Guidelines on Academic Integrity. This may include, but is not limited to, the confiscation of the examination of any individual suspected of violating University Policy. Furthermore, no student may bring any unauthorized materials to an exam, including dictionaries and programmable calculators.

To learn more about Academic Integrity, visit the Academic Integrity Guide
 for an overview of the topic. For hands-on practice, complete the Academic Integrity Modules

.
Use of Generative AI Tools in the MDS Program

Generative AI tools (such as OpenAI GPT-5 and Coursera Coach) can serve as on-demand learning assistants that enhance and accelerate students’ progress when used appropriately and purposefully. To both empower students with emerging technologies and ensure academic integrity, the Master of Data Science (MDS) Program adopts the following policy for all courses.
Generative AI Statement

The use of generative AI tools, including Coursera Coach, is permitted with specific limitations.

Acceptable uses include:

    Assisting with understanding course content, code, and problem explanations.

    Supporting note-taking and concept review.

    Brainstorming ideas for assignments or projects.

    Revising or refining work that you have written.

    Preparing for assessments with AI-generated practice questions.

    Exploring connections between course concepts and real-world applications. Disability Services

If you have a disability for which you are or may be requesting an accommodation, you are encouraged to contact both your instructor and Disability Resources and Services

 (DRS), 140 William Pitt Union, (412) 648-7890, drsrecep@pitt.edu, (412) 228-5347 for P3 ASL users, as early as possible in the term. DRS will verify your disability and determine reasonable accommodations for this course.
Accessibility

Please see Coursera’s Accessibility Policy. 

Civil Rights and Title IX

. You may also choose to report this to a faculty/staff member; they are required to communicate this to the University’s Office of Institutional Engagement and Wellbeing. If you wish to maintain complete confidentiality, you may also contact the University Counseling Center (412-648-7930).
Religious Observances

<p data-start="225" data-end="375">Perfect — we can absolutely run this 
like a real project: you’re the domain expert + decision-maker, I’m the 
“method + structure + polish + QA” layer.</p>
<p data-start="377" data-end="499">Here’s a clean “course operating system” you can set up once, then reuse for every module and each of the 3 major reports.</p>
<hr data-start="501" data-end="504">
<h2 data-start="506" data-end="563">1) What matters for your grade (so we optimize effort)</h2>
<p data-start="564" data-end="574">Big rocks:</p>
<ul data-start="575" data-end="753">
<li data-start="575" data-end="673">
<p data-start="577" data-end="673"><strong data-start="577" data-end="608">Assignments 1–3 = 90% total</strong> (each has <strong data-start="619" data-end="639">two parts at 15%</strong> → each part is basically an exam)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="674" data-end="700">
<p data-start="676" data-end="700"><strong data-start="676" data-end="700">Process diaries = 6%</strong></p>
</li>
<li data-start="701" data-end="719">
<p data-start="703" data-end="719"><strong data-start="703" data-end="719">Quizzes = 3%</strong></p>
</li>
<li data-start="720" data-end="753">
<p data-start="722" data-end="753">Discussions + Assignment 0 = 1%</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="755" data-end="915">Translation: <strong data-start="768" data-end="820">never take a late penalty on any assignment part</strong>. A 10% late penalty on a 15%-weight part is a <strong data-start="867" data-end="914">1.5% hit to your final course grade per day</strong>.</p>
<p data-start="917" data-end="1041">Also: deadlines are <strong data-start="937" data-end="952">11:59 PM ET</strong>, which is <strong data-start="963" data-end="978">10:59 PM CT</strong> for you. Build your personal deadline as <strong data-start="1020" data-end="1040">the night before</strong>.</p>
<hr data-start="1043" data-end="1046">
<h2 data-start="1048" data-end="1104">2) Your course map (CRISP-DM aligned to deliverables)</h2>
<p data-start="1105" data-end="1243"><strong data-start="1105" data-end="1130">Unit 1 (Modules 1–5):</strong> Foundation + Business/Data Understanding<br data-start="1171" data-end="1174">
➡️ <strong data-start="1177" data-end="1202">Module 5 deliverable:</strong> <em data-start="1203" data-end="1243">Business and Data Understanding Report</em></p>
<p data-start="1245" data-end="1361"><strong data-start="1245" data-end="1270">Unit 2 (Modules 6–9):</strong> Data Prep + Modeling<br data-start="1291" data-end="1294">
➡️ <strong data-start="1297" data-end="1322">Module 9 deliverable:</strong> <em data-start="1323" data-end="1361">Data Preparation and Modeling Report</em></p>
<p data-start="1363" data-end="1461"><strong data-start="1363" data-end="1390">Unit 3 (Modules 10–13):</strong> Evaluation + Deployment<br data-start="1414" data-end="1417">
➡️ <strong data-start="1420" data-end="1446">Module 13 deliverable:</strong> <em data-start="1447" data-end="1461">Final Report</em></p>
<p data-start="1463" data-end="1524"><strong data-start="1463" data-end="1477">Module 14:</strong> wrap + synthesis (usually polishing/packaging)</p>
<hr data-start="1526" data-end="1529">
<h2 data-start="1531" data-end="1591">3) The system: one repo, repeatable templates, zero chaos</h2>
<h3 data-start="1592" data-end="1657">Recommended folder structure (simple, professional, scalable)</h3>
<pre class="overflow-visible! px-0!" data-start="1658" data-end="2024"><div class="contain-inline-size rounded-2xl corner-superellipse/1.1 relative bg-token-sidebar-surface-primary"><div class="flex items-center text-token-text-secondary px-4 py-2 text-xs font-sans justify-between h-9 bg-token-sidebar-surface-primary select-none rounded-t-2xl corner-t-superellipse/1.1">markdown</div><div class="sticky top-[calc(var(--sticky-padding-top)+9*var(--spacing))]"><div class="absolute end-0 bottom-0 flex h-9 items-center pe-2"><div class="bg-token-bg-elevated-secondary text-token-text-secondary flex items-center gap-4 rounded-sm px-2 font-sans text-xs"><button class="flex gap-1 items-center select-none py-1" aria-label="Copy"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#ce3544" fill="currentColor"></use></svg>Copy code</button></div></div></div><div class="overflow-y-auto p-4" dir="ltr"><code class="whitespace-pre!"><span><span>case-studies-capstone/

  data/
<span class="hljs-code">    raw/
    interim/

</span>

    M02_*.ipynb

</span>

    features.py

</span>

</span>

</span></span></code></div></div></pre>
<p data-start="2026" data-end="2177">If you already use Git at work: 
same playbook here. If not, no problem — but even basic commits help 
your process diary a ton (“what changed and why”).</p>
<hr data-start="2179" data-end="2182">
<h2 data-start="2184" data-end="2247">4) One master tracker you update as you go (copy/paste this)</h2>
<p data-start="2248" data-end="2278">Create <code data-start="2255" data-end="2277">00_master_tracker.md</code>:</p>
<h3 data-start="2280" data-end="2321">Module checklist (Definition of Done)</h3>
<p data-start="2322" data-end="2338">For each module:</p>
<ul class="contains-task-list" data-start="2339" data-end="2617">
<li class="task-list-item" data-start="2339" data-end="2372">
<p data-start="2345" data-end="2372"><input disabled="disabled" type="checkbox"> Watch/read module content</p>
</li>
<li class="task-list-item" data-start="2373" data-end="2405">
<p data-start="2379" data-end="2405"><input disabled="disabled" type="checkbox"> Notes captured (bullets)</p>
</li>
<li class="task-list-item" data-start="2406" data-end="2453">
<p data-start="2412" data-end="2453"><input disabled="disabled" type="checkbox"> Notebook updated (code runs top→bottom)</p>
</li>
<li class="task-list-item" data-start="2454" data-end="2522">
<p data-start="2460" data-end="2522"><input disabled="disabled" type="checkbox"> “Report snippets” updated (1–2 paragraphs or a table/figure)</p>
</li>
<li class="task-list-item" data-start="2523" data-end="2556">
<p data-start="2529" data-end="2556"><input disabled="disabled" type="checkbox"> Quiz done (if applicable)</p>
</li>
<li class="task-list-item" data-start="2557" data-end="2617">
<p data-start="2563" data-end="2617"><input disabled="disabled" type="checkbox"> Diary entry updated (only for the 3 diary checkpoints)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 data-start="2619" data-end="2633">Milestones</h3>
<ul data-start="2634" data-end="2814">
<li data-start="2634" data-end="2687">
<p data-start="2636" data-end="2687"><strong data-start="2636" data-end="2650">M05 Report</strong>: draft → revise → final (buffer day)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2688" data-end="2741">
<p data-start="2690" data-end="2741"><strong data-start="2690" data-end="2704">M09 Report</strong>: draft → revise → final (buffer day)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2742" data-end="2814">
<p data-start="2744" data-end="2814"><strong data-start="2744" data-end="2757">M13 Final</strong>: outline locked → draft → polish → final QA (buffer day)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="2816" data-end="2819">
<h2 data-start="2821" data-end="2878">5) The “snippets” trick: write the reports <em data-start="2867" data-end="2878">as you go</em></h2>
<p data-start="2879" data-end="3055">Instead of waiting until Module 
5/9/13 and panic-writing, you maintain a living set of “report snippets”
 each module. Then your report becomes assembly + polish, not invention.</p>
<h3 data-start="3057" data-end="3099">Snippet types (small, reusable blocks)</h3>
<ul data-start="3100" data-end="3558">
<li data-start="3100" data-end="3163">
<p data-start="3102" data-end="3163"><strong data-start="3102" data-end="3127">Decision + rationale:</strong> “We chose X because…, tradeoff is…”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3164" data-end="3231">
<p data-start="3166" data-end="3231"><strong data-start="3166" data-end="3185">Assumption log:</strong> what you’re assuming + how you’ll validate it</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3232" data-end="3296">
<p data-start="3234" data-end="3296"><strong data-start="3234" data-end="3253">Data inventory:</strong> tables/files, row counts, keys, time range</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3297" data-end="3365">
<p data-start="3299" data-end="3365"><strong data-start="3299" data-end="3325">Data quality findings:</strong> missingness, duplicates, weird outliers</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3366" data-end="3432">
<p data-start="3368" data-end="3432"><strong data-start="3368" data-end="3385">Feature list:</strong> inputs → engineered features → why they matter</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3433" data-end="3498">
<p data-start="3435" data-end="3498"><strong data-start="3435" data-end="3450">Model card:</strong> algorithm, hyperparams, metrics, error analysis</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3499" data-end="3558">
<p data-start="3501" data-end="3558"><strong data-start="3501" data-end="3529">Stakeholder translation:</strong> “So what?” in business terms</p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="3560" data-end="3563">
<h2 data-start="3565" data-end="3604">6) Report templates (ready to paste)</h2>
<h3 data-start="3605" data-end="3678">Module 5 — Business &amp; Data Understanding Report (suggested structure)</h3>
<p data-start="3679" data-end="3701"><strong data-start="3679" data-end="3701">1. Problem framing</strong></p>
<ul data-start="3702" data-end="3908">
<li data-start="3702" data-end="3736">
<p data-start="3704" data-end="3736">Business problem (plain English)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3737" data-end="3781">
<p data-start="3739" data-end="3781">Stakeholders + decisions they need to make</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3782" data-end="3863">
<p data-start="3784" data-end="3863"><strong data-start="3784" data-end="3810">Data science objective</strong> (what you’re predicting/classifying/segmenting/etc.)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3864" data-end="3908">
<p data-start="3866" data-end="3908"><strong data-start="3866" data-end="3885">Success metrics</strong> (business + technical)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="3910" data-end="3937"><strong data-start="3910" data-end="3937">2. Situation assessment</strong></p>
<ul data-start="3938" data-end="4086">
<li data-start="3938" data-end="3989">
<p data-start="3940" data-end="3989">Constraints (time, data access, privacy, compute)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3990" data-end="4054">
<p data-start="3992" data-end="4054">Risks (bias, leakage, measurement error, shifting definitions)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4055" data-end="4086">
<p data-start="4057" data-end="4086">Assumptions + validation plan</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4088" data-end="4113"><strong data-start="4088" data-end="4113">3. Data understanding</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4114" data-end="4299">
<li data-start="4114" data-end="4140">
<p data-start="4116" data-end="4140">Data sources + ownership</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4141" data-end="4193">
<p data-start="4143" data-end="4193">Data dictionary starter (key fields, units, grain)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4194" data-end="4258">
<p data-start="4196" data-end="4258">Initial EDA highlights (distributions, missingness, anomalies)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4259" data-end="4299">
<p data-start="4261" data-end="4299">Initial hypotheses / questions to test</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4301" data-end="4318"><strong data-start="4301" data-end="4318">4. Next steps</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4319" data-end="4379">
<li data-start="4319" data-end="4379">
<p data-start="4321" data-end="4379">What you will do in Data Prep + Modeling (Module 6–9 plan)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="4381" data-end="4384">
<h3 data-start="4386" data-end="4428">Module 9 — Data Prep &amp; Modeling Report</h3>
<p data-start="4429" data-end="4448"><strong data-start="4429" data-end="4448">1. Prep summary</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4449" data-end="4556">
<li data-start="4449" data-end="4476">
<p data-start="4451" data-end="4476">Cleaning steps (what/why)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4477" data-end="4513">
<p data-start="4479" data-end="4513">Exclusions/inclusions (and impact)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4514" data-end="4556">
<p data-start="4516" data-end="4556">Train/validation/test strategy (and why)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4558" data-end="4584"><strong data-start="4558" data-end="4584">2. Feature engineering</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4585" data-end="4660">
<li data-start="4585" data-end="4611">
<p data-start="4587" data-end="4611">Feature list + rationale</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4612" data-end="4660">
<p data-start="4614" data-end="4660">Leakage checks (explicitly state what you did)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4662" data-end="4677"><strong data-start="4662" data-end="4677">3. Modeling</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4678" data-end="4780">
<li data-start="4678" data-end="4703">
<p data-start="4680" data-end="4703">Baseline model (always)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4704" data-end="4737">
<p data-start="4706" data-end="4737">Candidate models + why selected</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4738" data-end="4780">
<p data-start="4740" data-end="4780">Hyperparameter approach (simple is fine)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4782" data-end="4796"><strong data-start="4782" data-end="4796">4. Results</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4797" data-end="4908">
<li data-start="4797" data-end="4831">
<p data-start="4799" data-end="4831">Primary metrics + interpretation</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4832" data-end="4873">
<p data-start="4834" data-end="4873">Error analysis (where it fails and why)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4874" data-end="4908">
<p data-start="4876" data-end="4908">Fairness/bias checks if relevant</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4910" data-end="4931"><strong data-start="4910" data-end="4931">5. Recommendation</strong></p>
<ul data-start="4932" data-end="4991">
<li data-start="4932" data-end="4991">
<p data-start="4934" data-end="4991">What model you’d move forward with and what you’d monitor</p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="4993" data-end="4996">

data-[multiline]:py-3 rounded-se-lg max-w-[var(--user-chat-width,70%)]" data-multiline=""><div class="whitespace-pre-wrap">Introduction to CRISP-DM """Welcome to our introduction to CRISP-DM, one of the most widely used frameworks for data science projects. By the end of this video, you'll understand how this powerful methodology can guide you from identifying business problems to deploying data-driven solutions. Let me start by sharing what you'll learn in this video. First, you'll be able to identify the six phases of CRISP-DM and understand how they connect in a cyclical process. Second, you'll understand the hierarchical structure that makes this methodology so flexible. And third, you'll recognize why using this standardized approach like CRISP-DM is crucial for successful data science projects. Throughout this video series, we'll explore CRISP-DM through Steelbridge Sports, a family-owned sporting goods retailer in Steelbridgeford, a vibrant mid-sized city famous for the iconic Steelbridge that spans the Clearwater River and connects to its historic downtown with residential neighborhoods. 
For 30 years, Steelbridge Sports has thrived by serving their community through 12 physical stores and a growing online presence. But now they face their biggest challenge yet, intense competition from national online retailers that threaten their local market dominance. Steelbridge Sports recognizes their abundance of data is a competitive advantage, and they want to use it to develop new business strategies. This is where CRISP-DM comes in. CRISP-DM stands for Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining. It's a proven methodology that provides structure and guidance for data science projects across any industry. The power of CRISP-DM lies in its six interconnected phases that form a complete life cycle for data science projects. 
Let me walk you through each one using Steelbridge Sports as our example. First is business understanding, where Steelbridge Sports would define exactly how they want to compete with online retailers and set specific measurable goals for their data science initiative. Second comes data understanding, where they explore what data they actually have from point-of-sale transactions to customer loyalty programs and website analytics. Third is data preparation, often the most time-consuming phase, where Steelbridge Sports would clean, integrate, and transform their scattered retail data into a format that's ready for analysis. Fourth is modeling, where they build recommendation engines, demand forecasting models, and customer segmentation algorithms to drive their competitive strategy. Fifth is evaluation, where they assess whether their models actually deliver the business value they promised, and not just technical accuracy, but real impact on customer retention and sales. And sixth is deployment, where they implement these models into their actual business operations from personalized website recommendations to inventory management systems. 
And here's what makes CRISP-DM truly powerful. It's not a linear process. Notice the arrows in our diagram? They show that you can constantly move back and forth between the phases. When Steelbridge Sports discovers data quality issues during modeling, they return to data preparation. When evaluation reveals new business opportunities, they cycle back to business understanding. This brings us to CRISP-DM's hierarchical structure, which makes it adaptable to any project. 
At the top level, we have six phases. Each phase contains generic tasks that apply to all data science projects. These tasks can then be specialized for specific situations, like retail analytics versus healthcare or manufacturing. Finally, each actual project creates process instances that document what really happened. Let's see this hierarchy in action with Steelbridge Sports. In the business understanding phase, there's a generic task called Determine Business Objectives. For Steelbridge Sports specifically, this becomes Define Competitive Strategy Against Online Retailers. 
Their actual process instance might document exactly how they conducted stakeholder interviews and analyzed market data. So why does this standardized approach matter? First, it ensures you don't skip important tasks and jump straight to modeling without understanding the business problem. Second, it provides a common language for teams to communicate about project progress. Third, it captures lessons learned that can improve future projects. Think about Steelbridge Sports again. Without CRISP-DM, they might have built sophisticated algorithms that don't address their business needs or deployed models without proper monitoring systems. 
CRISP-DM ensures they stay focused on creating genuine business value. Throughout this course, we'll dive deep into each phase, exploring the specific tasks, outputs, and best practices that make CRISP-DM so effective. You'll see how our fictional company, Steelbridge Sports, navigates each challenge using the CRISP-DM process to guide their project. In this video, we've introduced the six phases of CRISP-DM methodology, explored its hierarchical structure that adapts to any project, and seen why standardized approaches are critical for data science success. More importantly, you've met Steelbridge Sports and began to understand how CRISP-DM can guide them from competitive threat to data-driven success. In our next video, we'll dive into the business understanding phase where CRISP-DM transforms their competitive advantage into specific data science objectives. You'll learn exactly how to align technical work with business goals, the foundation of every successful data science project. """  The CRISP-DM Framework """The CRISP-DM Framework
Introduction

The Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) stands as one of the most widely adopted methodologies for conducting data science projects across industries. This framework provides a structured approach to transforming business problems into data-driven solutions, ensuring that data science work remains aligned with organizational objectives and follows best practices developed through extensive real-world experience.
Origins and Development

CRISP-DM was conceived in late 1996 by three pioneers in the data mining field who recognized a critical need in the emerging discipline. At that time, DaimlerChrysler (then Daimler-Benz) was already applying data mining in business operations, SPSS had been providing data mining services since 1990 and launched the first commercial data mining workbench (Clementine) in 1994, and NCR had established teams of data mining consultants to service their Teradata data warehouse customers.

These industry veterans faced a crucial question: Were they doing data mining right? As the field showed signs of explosive growth, they worried that every new adopter would have to learn through trial and error, as they initially had. From a supplier's perspective, they needed to demonstrate that data mining was sufficiently mature to be adopted as a key business process.

The solution was ambitious: develop a standard process model that was non-proprietary, freely available, and based on real-world experience rather than academic theory. A consortium was formed including NCR Systems Engineering Copenhagen, DaimlerChrysler AG, SPSS Inc., and OHRA Verzekeringen en Bank Groep B.V., with funding from the European Commission.

The development process was notably collaborative and practical. Rather than being created by elite committees behind closed doors, CRISP-DM emerged from the experiences of practitioners across industries. The consortium created the CRISP-DM Special Interest Group (SIG), which grew to over 200 members and held workshops in Amsterdam, London, New York, and Brussels. This collaborative approach ensured that the methodology reflected diverse, real-world experience rather than theoretical ideals.  
Industry Adoption and Impact

CRISP-DM's success stems from its practical foundation. The methodology has been validated across numerous projects spanning multiple industries and business problems. Professional services groups at major technology companies have adopted CRISP-DM for customer engagements, and it has become the de facto standard referenced in invitations to tender and RFP documents.

The framework's industry-neutral, tool-neutral, and application-neutral design has contributed to its widespread adoption. Unlike methodologies tied to specific software platforms or business domains, CRISP-DM provides a universal structure that adapts to various contexts while maintaining consistency in approach.
Required Readings

To build upon this overview, please read the following sections from the CRISP-DM 1.0 Guide:

    Introduction (Section I): Pages 6-9

        The CRISP-DM methodology

        Mapping generic models to specialized models

        Description of parts

    The CRISP-DM Reference Model Overview (Section II): Pages 10-12

        Overview of the six phases and their relationships

        Understanding the cyclical nature of the process

These readings will provide the detailed foundation for understanding how CRISP-DM's hierarchical structure translates into practical project guidance, preparing you for the phase-by-phase exploration that follows in subsequent modules.

The CRISP-DM Structure: A Hierarchical Process Model

One of CRISP-DM's key innovations is its hierarchical structure, which provides guidance at multiple levels of detail. Understanding this structure is crucial for effective application of the methodology.
Four Levels of Abstraction

The CRISP-DM methodology operates at four distinct levels, moving from general to specific:

    Phase Level: The highest level organizes the data mining process into six major phases, each with distinct objectives and outcomes.

    Generic Task Level: Each phase consists of several generic tasks that are intended to be complete and stable enough to cover all possible data mining situations and remain valid even as new techniques emerge.

    Specialized Task Level: This level describes how generic tasks should be carried out in specific situations. For example, while "clean data" is a generic task, the specialized level describes how this differs when cleaning numeric versus categorical values, or when the problem type is clustering versus predictive modeling.

    Process Instance Level: This represents the actual record of actions, decisions, and results from a specific data mining engagement, organized according to the higher levels but reflecting what actually happened in practice.

This hierarchical approach allows CRISP-DM to provide both high-level guidance and detailed, context-specific direction. The generic level ensures broad applicability, while specialized levels allow adaptation to specific circumstances.
Four level breakdown of the CRISP-DM methodology showing the hierarchical structure.

Figure 1 - Four level breakdown of the CRISP-DM methodology showing the hierarchical structure from Phases to Generic Tasks to Specialized Tasks to Process Instances. Image Source: The CRISP-DM Guide
The Six-Phase Lifecycle
CRISP-DM Model showing the cyclical nature with six interconnected phases and arrows indicating dependence.

Figure 2 - Phases of the CRISP-DM reference model showing the cyclical nature with six interconnected phases and arrows indicating dependencies. 

The CRISP-DM process consists of six interconnected phases that form a cyclical methodology:

    Business Understanding: Converting business problems into data mining objectives

    Data Understanding: Becoming familiar with the data and identifying quality issues

    Data Preparation: Constructing the final dataset for modeling

    Modeling: Applying various modeling techniques to extract patterns

    Evaluation: Assessing models against business objectives

    Deployment: Implementing data mining results into business operations

Generic tasks and outputs of the CRISP-DM reference model showing the detailed breakdown of each phase.

Figure 3 - Generic tasks (bold) and outputs (italic) of the CRISP-DM reference model showing the detailed breakdown of each phase with specific tasks and deliverables. Image Source: The CRISP-DM Guide
Cyclical and Iterative Nature

Unlike linear project methodologies, CRISP-DM explicitly recognizes the cyclical nature of data science work. The sequence of phases is not rigid—moving back and forth between phases is not only expected but necessary. The arrows in the CRISP-DM lifecycle diagram indicate the most important and frequent dependencies, but relationships can exist between any phases depending on project specifics.

The outer circle in the CRISP-DM diagram symbolizes the cyclical nature of data mining itself. Projects don't end with deployment; lessons learned and deployed solutions often trigger new business questions, leading to subsequent data mining processes that benefit from previous experiences.
Focus on Documentation and Outputs

One of CRISP-DM's distinguishing characteristics is its systematic emphasis on documentation and deliverables. Unlike methodologies that focus primarily on technical processes, CRISP-DM recognizes that successful data science projects require comprehensive documentation for communication, reproducibility, and knowledge transfer.
Structured Deliverables

Each phase in CRISP-DM produces specific, well-defined outputs that serve multiple purposes:

    Communication: Enable clear dialogue between technical teams and business stakeholders

    Decision-making: Provide concrete artifacts for project review and approval processes

    Knowledge preservation: Capture insights and decisions for future reference and similar projects

    Quality assurance: Create checkpoints for validating work before proceeding to subsequent phases

For example, the Business Understanding phase produces not just informal discussions but formal deliverables including background documentation, explicit business objectives and success criteria, resource inventories, and detailed project plans. This documentation discipline ensures that all stakeholders maintain alignment throughout the project lifecycle.
Cross-referencing and Dependencies

The CRISP-DM guide includes detailed cross-references showing how outputs from one phase become inputs to subsequent phases. This systematic approach to information flow helps practitioners understand not just what to produce, but how each deliverable contributes to the overall project success. The methodology recognizes that quality outputs at each phase directly impact the effectiveness of all subsequent work.
Reporting Framework

CRISP-DM provides specific guidance on report structures and contents, acknowledging that different audiences require different types of documentation. The framework distinguishes between technical documentation for practitioners and executive summaries for business stakeholders, ensuring that insights reach appropriate audiences in accessible formats.
CRISP-DM Today

More than two decades after its initial development, CRISP-DM remains remarkably relevant in the modern data science landscape, though its application has evolved alongside technological advances and organizational maturity.
Enduring Relevance

Despite significant changes in technology—from traditional data mining tools to modern machine learning platforms, from structured databases to big data ecosystems—CRISP-DM's process-oriented approach has proven remarkably durable. The fundamental challenges it addresses—aligning technical work with business objectives, managing complex iterative projects, ensuring quality through structured approaches—remain as relevant today as they were in 1999.
Contemporary Alternatives

While newer methodologies have emerged—such as KDD (Knowledge Discovery in Databases), SEMMA (Sample, Explore, Modify, Model, Assess), and various proprietary frameworks—CRISP-DM maintains its position as the most widely recognized standard. Its open, non-proprietary nature and industry-neutral design continue to make it attractive for organizations seeking a proven, standardized approach.
Current Applications

Today's data science teams often use CRISP-DM as:

    A common vocabulary for discussing project phases and deliverables

    A framework for structuring project proposals and progress reports

    A training tool for new data scientists learning systematic approaches

    A quality assurance checklist ensuring comprehensive project coverage

Why CRISP-DM Matters

The framework addresses several critical challenges in data science:

    Alignment: Ensures data science work remains connected to business objectives

    Structure: Provides clear organization for complex, multi-faceted projects

    Communication: Offers common vocabulary for diverse stakeholders

    Quality: Incorporates best practices developed through extensive real-world experience

    Adaptability: Flexible enough to accommodate various industries, problems, and technologies

The genius of CRISP-DM lies in its combination of structure and flexibility, providing enough guidance to ensure quality and consistency while allowing adaptation to the vast diversity of data science wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="132">Alright — Module 1 is basically teaching you <strong data-start="45" data-end="79">how to think + how to document</strong>, so the rest of the course becomes paint-by-numbers.</p>
<p data-start="134" data-end="309">Below is a “working cheat sheet” you can reuse for every case, plus a super practical way to turn CRISP-DM into your <strong data-start="251" data-end="268">course binder</strong> (reports + process diaries + notebooks).</p>
<p data-start="311" data-end="411">(Primary source: the CRISP-DM 1.0 guide excerpt you uploaded.) <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
<hr data-start="413" data-end="416">
<h2 data-start="418" data-end="489">1) The 2 diagrams you posted (what they <em data-start="461" data-end="471">actually</em> mean in practice)</h2>
<h3 data-start="491" data-end="550">A) The big circle: CRISP-DM is <strong data-start="526" data-end="538">cyclical</strong>, not linear</h3>
<p data-start="551" data-end="982">Your second image is the money shot: you’re expected to move <strong data-start="612" data-end="630">back and forth</strong>
 between phases (especially Business ↔ Data Understanding, and Data Prep
 ↔ Modeling). The guide explicitly says the phase sequence is <strong data-start="764" data-end="777">not rigid</strong>
 and that backtracking is “always required,” with the outer ring 
symbolizing that the work doesn’t “end” at deployment—deployment 
triggers the next round of questions. <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
<p data-start="984" data-end="1193"><strong data-start="984" data-end="1007">Course translation:</strong> if you discover a data limitation in Module 4/5, you <em data-start="1061" data-end="1069">should</em> revise your business objective phrasing, scope, success criteria, etc. That’s not failure — it’s correct CRISP-DM behavior.</p>
<h3 data-start="1195" data-end="1255">B) The “4-level hierarchy” diagram: it’s a <strong data-start="1242" data-end="1255">zoom lens</strong></h3>
<p data-start="1256" data-end="1311">Your first image is showing four levels of abstraction:</p>
<ol data-start="1313" data-end="1576">
<li data-start="1313" data-end="1344">
<p data-start="1316" data-end="1344"><strong data-start="1316" data-end="1326">Phases</strong> (6 big buckets)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1345" data-end="1404">
<p data-start="1348" data-end="1404"><strong data-start="1348" data-end="1365">Generic tasks</strong> (stable checklist inside each phase)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1405" data-end="1483">
<p data-start="1408" data-end="1483"><strong data-start="1408" data-end="1429">Specialized tasks</strong> (how <em data-start="1435" data-end="1440">you</em> execute tasks for this specific context)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1484" data-end="1576">
<p data-start="1487" data-end="1576"><strong data-start="1487" data-end="1507">Process instance</strong> (the actual record of what happened: decisions, iterations, results)</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p data-start="1578" data-end="1727">CRISP-DM is very explicit that the step-by-step view is <em data-start="1634" data-end="1645">idealized</em>; real projects reorder steps and backtrack. <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
<p data-start="1729" data-end="1903"><strong data-start="1729" data-end="1752">Course translation:</strong> your <strong data-start="1758" data-end="1775">process diary</strong> is literally the <em data-start="1793" data-end="1811">process instance</em> layer. If you document decisions + why you changed course, you’re doing CRISP-DM correctly.</p>
<h3 data-start="1905" data-end="1982">C) The “tasks + outputs” table: this is your <strong data-start="1954" data-end="1982">report outline generator</strong></h3>
<p data-start="1983" data-end="2282">Your third image lists the generic 
tasks per phase and the expected outputs (e.g., Business Understanding →
 determine objectives / assess situation / data mining goals / project 
plan; Data Understanding → collect/describe/explore/verify quality; 
etc.). That’s basically the skeleton of Modules 1–13.</p>
<hr data-start="2284" data-end="2287">
<h2 data-start="2289" data-end="2360">2) Reference Model vs User Guide (why the reading keeps saying this)</h2>
<p data-start="2361" data-end="2395">CRISP-DM splits horizontally into:</p>
<ul data-start="2397" data-end="2531">
<li data-start="2397" data-end="2466">
<p data-start="2399" data-end="2466"><strong data-start="2399" data-end="2419">Reference model:</strong> “what to do” overview (phases, tasks, outputs)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2467" data-end="2531">
<p data-start="2469" data-end="2531"><strong data-start="2469" data-end="2484">User guide:</strong> “how to do it” (tips, hints, details per task)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="2533" data-end="2626">So: reference model = checklist; user guide = playbook. <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
<p data-start="2628" data-end="2742"><strong data-start="2628" data-end="2644">Course hack:</strong> use the reference model as your table of contents, then write your report sections in that order.</p>
<hr data-start="2744" data-end="2747">
<h2 data-start="2749" data-end="2809">3) Mapping generic → specialized (how you “make it real”)</h2>
<p data-start="2810" data-end="2902">CRISP-DM says your <em data-start="2829" data-end="2838">context</em> drives how you specialize tasks. It lists 4 context dimensions:</p>
<ul data-start="2904" data-end="3153">
<li data-start="2904" data-end="2955">
<p data-start="2906" data-end="2955"><strong data-start="2906" data-end="2928">Application domain</strong> (retail, healthcare, etc.)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2956" data-end="3018">
<p data-start="2958" data-end="3018"><strong data-start="2958" data-end="2974">Problem type</strong> (classification, prediction, segmentation…)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3019" data-end="3072">
<p data-start="3021" data-end="3072"><strong data-start="3021" data-end="3042">Technical aspects</strong> (missingness, outliers, etc.)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3073" data-end="3153">
<p data-start="3075" data-end="3153"><strong data-start="3075" data-end="3095">Tools/techniques</strong> (what you’re using) <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="3155" data-end="3198">And it gives an actual “how to map” recipe:</p>
<ul data-start="3200" data-end="3415">
<li data-start="3200" data-end="3224">
<p data-start="3202" data-end="3224">Analyze your context</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3225" data-end="3254">
<p data-start="3227" data-end="3254">Remove what doesn’t apply</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3255" data-end="3294">
<p data-start="3257" data-end="3294">Add what’s specific to your context</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3295" data-end="3338">
<p data-start="3297" data-end="3338">Specialize/instantiate generic contents</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3339" data-end="3415">
<p data-start="3341" data-end="3415">Optionally rename things for clarity <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="3417" data-end="3599"><strong data-start="3417" data-end="3440">Course translation:</strong> Steelbridge Sports is the “generic story,” but your report needs to show the <em data-start="3518" data-end="3539">specialized mapping</em> for the specific dataset + business objectives in the case.</p>
<hr data-start="3601" data-end="3604">
<h2 data-start="3606" data-end="3694">4) Your Module 1 deliverable kit (set this up once and you’re basically done forever)</h2>
<p data-start="3695" data-end="3793">Create these 3 living docs (markdown is fine). They’ll feed <strong data-start="3755" data-end="3778">Module 5, 9, and 13</strong> automatically.</p>
<h3 data-start="3795" data-end="3864">Doc A — Assumptions + Risks Log (Business Understanding backbone)</h3>
<p data-start="3865" data-end="3877">Each row is:</p>
<ul data-start="3878" data-end="3996">
<li data-start="3878" data-end="3890">
<p data-start="3880" data-end="3890">Assumption</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3891" data-end="3915">
<p data-start="3893" data-end="3915">Why you’re assuming it</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3916" data-end="3931">
<p data-start="3918" data-end="3931">Risk if wrong</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3932" data-end="3964">
<p data-start="3934" data-end="3964">How you’ll test/validate later</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3965" data-end="3996">
<p data-start="3967" data-end="3996">Status (open/validated/false)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="3998" data-end="4179"><strong data-start="3998" data-end="4019">Why this matters:</strong> CRISP-DM emphasizes documentation + iterative backtracking; this log is your “control panel” when you revise scope later. <span class="" data-state="closed"><span class="relative inline-flex items-center"><button class="ms-1 flex h-[25px] text-[10px] leading-[13px] rounded-xl corner-superellipse/1.1 items-center justify-center gap-1 px-2 relative text-token-text-secondary! hover:text-token-text-primary! hover:bg-token-bg-secondary dark:bg-token-main-surface-secondary dark:hover:bg-token-bg-secondary bg-[#f4f4f4] "><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="h-[16px] w-[16px] object-contain text-token-text-primary! flex-none icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#554074" fill="currentColor"></use></svg><p class="not-prose mt-0! mb-0! flex-auto truncate">CRISPMWP-1104-1C.qxd - crisp-dm…</p></button></span></span></p>
<h3 data-start="4181" data-end="4256">Doc B — Data Inventory + Data Quality Log (Data Understanding backbone)</h3>
<p data-start="4257" data-end="4276">Each dataset/table:</p>
<ul data-start="4277" data-end="4429">
<li data-start="4277" data-end="4302">
<p data-start="4279" data-end="4302">Grain (one row = what?)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4303" data-end="4315">
<p data-start="4305" data-end="4315">Key fields</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4316" data-end="4328">
<p data-start="4318" data-end="4328">Time range</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4329" data-end="4360">
<p data-start="4331" data-end="4360">Known missingness / weirdness</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4361" data-end="4392">
<p data-start="4363" data-end="4392">Join logic / leakage warnings</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4393" data-end="4429">
<p data-start="4395" data-end="4429">Notes (definitions that can shift)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 data-start="4431" data-end="4483">Doc C — Decision Log (Process instance backbone)</h3>
<p data-start="4484" data-end="4513">Every time you make a choice:</p>
<ul data-start="4514" data-end="4622">
<li data-start="4514" data-end="4524">
<p data-start="4516" data-end="4524">Decision</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4525" data-end="4550">
<p data-start="4527" data-end="4550">Alternatives considered</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4551" data-end="4569">
<p data-start="4553" data-end="4569">Why you chose it</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4570" data-end="4596">
<p data-start="4572" data-end="4596">What changed as a result</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4597" data-end="4622">
<p data-start="4599" data-end="4622">What you’d do next time</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="4624" data-end="4701"><strong data-start="4624" data-end="4657">This doc = Process Diary fuel</strong>. Same content, just rewritten as narrative.</p>
<hr data-start="4703" data-end="4706">
<h2 data-start="4708" data-end="4777">5) “Module 1: Definition of Done” (what you should walk away with)</h2>
<p data-start="4778" data-end="4868">If we’re being strict, after Module 1 you should be able to write (even without data yet):</p>
<ul data-start="4870" data-end="5179">
<li data-start="4870" data-end="4909">
<p data-start="4872" data-end="4909">The 6 CRISP-DM phases + why they loop</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4910" data-end="4953">
<p data-start="4912" data-end="4953">The 4-level hierarchy + how you’ll use it</p>
</li>
<li data-start="4954" data-end="5008">
<p data-start="4956" data-end="5008">The difference between reference model vs user guide</p>
</li>
<li data-start="5009" data-end="5084">
<p data-start="5011" data-end="5084">A plan for how you’ll document your process instance (diary/decision log)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="5085" data-end="5179">
<p data-start="5087" data-end="5179">A one-paragraph statement of <strong data-start="5116" data-end="5179">why a standardized methodology prevents ‘model-first’ chaos</strong></p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="5181" data-end="5184">
<h2 data-start="5186" data-end="5262">6) Quick practice questions (good quiz-prep without being “quiz answers”)</h2>
<ol data-start="5263" data-end="5709">
<li data-start="5263" data-end="5325">
<p data-start="5266" data-end="5325">Why is CRISP-DM described as cyclical rather than linear?</p>
</li>
<li data-start="5326" data-end="5424">
<p data-start="5329" data-end="5424">What’s the difference between a <strong data-start="5361" data-end="5377">generic task</strong> and a <strong data-start="5384" data-end="5404">specialized task</strong>? Give an example.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="5425" data-end="5532">
<p data-start="5428" data-end="5532">In your own words, what is a <strong data-start="5457" data-end="5477">process instance</strong>, and what artifacts in this course correspond to it?</p>
</li>
<li data-start="5533" data-end="5611">
<p data-start="5536" data-end="5611">What are the four “context dimensions” used to map generic → specialized?</p>
</li>
<li data-start="5612" data-end="5709">
<p data-start="5615" data-end="5709">Name one way a discovery in Data Understanding could force a change in Business Understanding.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p data-start="5711" data-end="5839">If you want, paste your answers and I’ll “grade” them like a TA: tighten wording, fix missing parts, and make them rubric-proof.</p>
<hr data-start="5841" data-end="5844">
<h2 data-start="5846" data-end="5888">7) Next move (Module 2 setup, no fluff)</h2>
<p data-start="5889" data-end="5994">Before you start Business Understanding (Modules 2–3), we’ll pre-build your <strong data-start="5965" data-end="5993">Module 5 report skeleton</strong>:</p>
<ul data-start="5996" data-end="6236">
<li data-start="5996" data-end="6029">
<p data-start="5998" data-end="6029">Business objective (measurable)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="6030" data-end="6057">
<p data-start="6032" data-end="6057">Business success criteria</p>
</li>
<li data-start="6058" data-end="6118">
<p data-start="6060" data-end="6118">Data mining objective (what you will predict/segment/etc.)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="6119" data-end="6159">
<p data-start="6121" data-end="6159">Data mining success criteria (metrics)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="6160" data-end="6208">
<p data-start="6162" data-end="6208">Constraints + risks + assumptions (from Log A)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="6209" data-end="6236">
<p data-start="6211" data-end="6236">Project plan (high level)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="6238" data-end="6623" data-is-last-node="" data-is-only-node="">When you’re ready, tell me one thing:<br>
<strong data-start="6276" data-end="6448">In the Steelbridge Sports 
storyline, what feels like the most “real” objective to you — 
churn/retention, product recommendations, demand forecasting, or 
something else?</strong><br data-start="6448" data-end="6451">
Pick one and we’ll map it cleanly into CRISP-DM language (business 
objective → data mining goal → success criteria) and you’ll have the 
backbone for the first major report.</p></div></div></div></div><div class="relative h-[60px]"><div class="absolute h-[60px]" style="opacity: 1;"><button class="not-prose group/footnote empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="51">Yeah — that Steelbridge moment is <em data-start="34" data-end="45">painfully</em> real:</p>
<p data-start="53" data-end="191">Leadership: “We need data.”<br data-start="80" data-end="83">
Analyst: “Cool… data for <strong data-start="108" data-end="125">what decision</strong>, with <strong data-start="132" data-end="151">what definition</strong>, measured <strong data-start="162" data-end="169">how</strong>, and used <strong data-start="180" data-end="189">where</strong>?”</p>
<p data-start="193" data-end="377">That dynamic happens because leadership often speaks in <strong data-start="249" data-end="261">outcomes</strong> (“compete with Amazon”), while analysts have to translate that into <strong data-start="330" data-end="376">operational decisions + measurable targets</strong>.</p>
<h3 data-start="379" data-end="440">Are analysts basically shadow leadership because of this?</h3>
<p data-start="441" data-end="513">In a lot of orgs: <strong data-start="459" data-end="513">functionally, yes — but only inside a narrow lane.</strong></p>
<p data-start="515" data-end="594">You’re “shadow leadership” when you’re doing these things (often by necessity):</p>
<ul data-start="595" data-end="1116">
<li data-start="595" data-end="711">
<p data-start="597" data-end="711"><strong data-start="597" data-end="625">Clarifying the decision:</strong> “What are we actually choosing? price, inventory, staffing, offers, store footprint?”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="712" data-end="801">
<p data-start="714" data-end="801"><strong data-start="714" data-end="743">Setting success criteria:</strong> “What counts as ‘better’ and when do we declare victory?”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="802" data-end="904">
<p data-start="804" data-end="904"><strong data-start="804" data-end="828">Defining the metric:</strong> “What exactly is ‘retention’? 30/90 days? active user? purchase frequency?”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="905" data-end="1014">
<p data-start="907" data-end="1014"><strong data-start="907" data-end="930">Constraining scope:</strong> “We can’t predict that with current data; here’s what we <em data-start="988" data-end="993">can</em> do with confidence.”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1015" data-end="1116">
<p data-start="1017" data-end="1116"><strong data-start="1017" data-end="1038">Creating options:</strong> “Here are 3 approaches with tradeoffs (fast/accurate/explainable). Pick one.”</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="1118" data-end="1234">That’s <em data-start="1125" data-end="1142">leadership work</em> (framing, prioritizing, tradeoffs), just focused on the <strong data-start="1199" data-end="1228">information + measurement</strong> side.</p>
<h3 data-start="1236" data-end="1299">The key distinction: decision authority vs decision shaping</h3>
<p data-start="1300" data-end="1437">Most analysts don’t have the authority to decide <em data-start="1349" data-end="1373">what the business does</em>, but strong analysts <strong data-start="1395" data-end="1433">shape what leadership <em data-start="1419" data-end="1424">can</em> decide</strong> by:</p>
<ul data-start="1438" data-end="1590">
<li data-start="1438" data-end="1464">
<p data-start="1440" data-end="1464">controlling definitions,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1465" data-end="1497">
<p data-start="1467" data-end="1497">controlling what’s measurable,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1498" data-end="1544">
<p data-start="1500" data-end="1544">controlling how uncertainty is communicated,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1545" data-end="1590">
<p data-start="1547" data-end="1590">and often controlling what’s even feasible.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="1592" data-end="1717">So you’re not “shadow leadership” in title, but you’re often <strong data-start="1653" data-end="1672">shadow strategy</strong>: you build the map leadership uses to steer.</p>
<h3 data-start="1719" data-end="1785">Why this happens (and why CRISP-DM is basically validating it)</h3>
<p data-start="1786" data-end="1894">CRISP-DM starts with Business Understanding <em data-start="1830" data-end="1842">on purpose</em> because jumping straight to “give me data” creates:</p>
<ul data-start="1895" data-end="2008">
<li data-start="1895" data-end="1913">
<p data-start="1897" data-end="1913">wrong objective,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1914" data-end="1929">
<p data-start="1916" data-end="1929">wrong metric,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1930" data-end="1952">
<p data-start="1932" data-end="1952">wrong dataset grain,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1953" data-end="1963">
<p data-start="1955" data-end="1963">leakage,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1964" data-end="2008">
<p data-start="1966" data-end="2008">and a model that’s impressive but useless.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="2010" data-end="2114">The framework is basically saying: <strong data-start="2045" data-end="2092">the analyst must force the translation step</strong> or the project fails.</p>
<h3 data-start="2116" data-end="2183">When this becomes a problem (the “analyst as de-facto PM” trap)</h3>
<p data-start="2184" data-end="2222">You become accidental leadership when:</p>
<ul data-start="2223" data-end="2390">
<li data-start="2223" data-end="2277">
<p data-start="2225" data-end="2277">requirements are vague (“make us more competitive”),</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2278" data-end="2326">
<p data-start="2280" data-end="2326">stakeholders won’t commit to success criteria,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2327" data-end="2390">
<p data-start="2329" data-end="2390">and you’re the only one who can connect ops → data → metrics.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="2392" data-end="2433">It’s powerful, but it can also turn into:</p>
<ul data-start="2434" data-end="2565">
<li data-start="2434" data-end="2477">
<p data-start="2436" data-end="2477">you owning the narrative <em data-start="2461" data-end="2466">and</em> the blame,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2478" data-end="2517">
<p data-start="2480" data-end="2517">endless rework due to shifting goals,</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2518" data-end="2565">
<p data-start="2520" data-end="2565">scope creep disguised as “one more question.”</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 data-start="2567" data-end="2606">The healthy version (what you want)</h3>
<p data-start="2607" data-end="2662">A good analyst relationship with leadership looks like:</p>
<ul data-start="2663" data-end="2899">
<li data-start="2663" data-end="2747">
<p data-start="2665" data-end="2747">Leadership owns <strong data-start="2681" data-end="2712">the objective + constraints</strong> (what matters, what can’t happen).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2748" data-end="2835">
<p data-start="2750" data-end="2835">Analyst owns <strong data-start="2763" data-end="2788">measurement + options</strong> (how to quantify, what’s possible, tradeoffs).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2836" data-end="2899">
<p data-start="2838" data-end="2899">Together you lock <strong data-start="2856" data-end="2876">success criteria</strong> before heavy modeling.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="2901" data-end="2904">
<h2 data-start="2906" data-end="2953">A practical line you can use (work + course)</h2>
<p data-start="2954" data-end="3001">When someone says “give me data,” respond with:</p>
<ol data-start="3003" data-end="3149">
<li data-start="3003" data-end="3041">
<p data-start="3006" data-end="3041">“What decision will this change?”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3042" data-end="3098">
<p data-start="3045" data-end="3098">“What does success look like (number + timeframe)?”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="3099" data-end="3149">
<p data-start="3102" data-end="3149">“What action will we take based on the result?”</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p data-start="3151" data-end="3250">If they can’t answer those, the right next step isn’t “more data.” It’s <strong data-start="3223" data-end="3249">Business Understanding</strong>.</p>
<hr data-start="3252" data-end="3255">
<p data-start="3257" data-end="3591" data-is-last-node="" data-is-only-node="">If you want, tell me what your <em data-start="3288" data-end="3294">real</em> version of Steelbridge is at work (even abstracted):<br data-start="3347" data-end="3350">
What’s the typical “give me data” request you get, and what decision are
 they actually trying to make? I’ll help you translate it into CRISP-DM 
language (objective → success criteria → data needs) so you can reuse it
 in your Module 5 report.</p></div></div></div></div><div class="z-0 flex min-h-[46px] justify-start"><div class="touch:-me-2 touch:-ms-3.5 -ms-2.5 -me-1 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-y-4 p-1 class="flex w-full flex-col gap-1 empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="90">100%. “No authority” is technically true on an org chart, but in the real world it’s like:</p>
<p data-start="92" data-end="202"><strong data-start="92" data-end="202">Authority = who signs the decision.<br data-start="129" data-end="132">
Influence = who defines the menu, the labels, and the calorie count.</strong></p>
<p data-start="204" data-end="273">If you control the options, you control a <em data-start="246" data-end="251">big</em> chunk of the outcome.</p>
<h3 data-start="275" data-end="315">Why the “options guy” has real power</h3>
<p data-start="316" data-end="409">When you say “these are your options,” you’re implicitly doing leadership work in three ways:</p>
<ol data-start="411" data-end="433">
<li data-start="411" data-end="433">
<p data-start="414" data-end="433"><strong data-start="414" data-end="433">Problem framing</strong></p>
</li>
</ol>
<ul data-start="434" data-end="610">
<li data-start="434" data-end="475">
<p data-start="436" data-end="475">Option A assumes the goal is retention.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="476" data-end="514">
<p data-start="478" data-end="514">Option B assumes the goal is margin.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="515" data-end="610">
<p data-start="517" data-end="610">Option C assumes the goal is throughput.<br>
Whichever framing you lead with becomes the default.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<ol start="2" data-start="612" data-end="718">
<li data-start="612" data-end="718">
<p data-start="615" data-end="718"><strong data-start="615" data-end="637">Constraint setting</strong><br>
Even if leadership <em data-start="657" data-end="664">could</em> choose anything, you’re narrowing to what’s feasible:</p>
</li>
</ol>
<ul data-start="719" data-end="868">
<li data-start="719" data-end="756">
<p data-start="721" data-end="756">“This is measurable with our data.”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="757" data-end="796">
<p data-start="759" data-end="796">“This will take 2 weeks vs 2 months.”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="797" data-end="868">
<p data-start="799" data-end="868">“This will require IT / workflow change.”<br>
Feasibility becomes policy.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<ol start="3" data-start="870" data-end="1119">
<li data-start="870" data-end="1119">
<p data-start="873" data-end="1119"><strong data-start="873" data-end="895">Success definition</strong><br>
If you define the metric and thresholds, you define what “good” looks like.<br>
A model that improves AUC by 0.03 sounds nice, but if it doesn’t change a
 decision, it’s noise. You’re the person who connects “metric” → 
“action.”</p>
</li>
</ol>
<h3 data-start="1121" data-end="1164">The quiet leverage: ordering + defaults</h3>
<p data-start="1165" data-end="1279">This is the part nobody says out loud: <strong data-start="1204" data-end="1239">the first option is the default</strong> unless someone is unusually thoughtful.</p>
<p data-start="1281" data-end="1327">So even without “authority,” you can steer by:</p>
<ul data-start="1328" data-end="1586">
<li data-start="1328" data-end="1383">
<p data-start="1330" data-end="1383"><strong data-start="1330" data-end="1350">Option ordering:</strong> lead with what you think is best</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1384" data-end="1445">
<p data-start="1386" data-end="1445"><strong data-start="1386" data-end="1397">Naming:</strong> “Safe baseline” vs “experimental high-variance”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1446" data-end="1515">
<p data-start="1448" data-end="1515"><strong data-start="1448" data-end="1460">Costing:</strong> time/effort/risk table makes some choices unattractive</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1516" data-end="1586">
<p data-start="1518" data-end="1586"><strong data-start="1518" data-end="1545">Default recommendation:</strong> “If you want my recommendation, it’s B.”</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="1588" data-end="1661">You’re basically doing the “decision architecture” version of leadership.</p>
<h3 data-start="1663" data-end="1714">The ethical line (important for the course too)</h3>
<p data-start="1715" data-end="1780">Influence is good when it’s transparent. It becomes sketchy when:</p>
<ul data-start="1781" data-end="1942">
<li data-start="1781" data-end="1860">
<p data-start="1783" data-end="1860">options are intentionally incomplete (“I left out C because I don’t like it”)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1861" data-end="1883">
<p data-start="1863" data-end="1883">tradeoffs are hidden</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1884" data-end="1942">
<p data-start="1886" data-end="1942">uncertainty is overstated/understated to push an outcome</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="1944" data-end="2011">A clean, defensible way to use your influence is to always include:</p>
<ul data-start="2012" data-end="2180">
<li data-start="2012" data-end="2036">
<p data-start="2014" data-end="2036"><strong data-start="2014" data-end="2036">2–4 viable options</strong></p>
</li>
<li data-start="2037" data-end="2057">
<p data-start="2039" data-end="2057">explicit tradeoffs</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2058" data-end="2089">
<p data-start="2060" data-end="2089">your recommendation <em data-start="2080" data-end="2089">and why</em></p>
</li>
<li data-start="2090" data-end="2180">
<p data-start="2092" data-end="2180">what would change your recommendation (data you’d need, a constraint that would flip it)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="2182" data-end="2290">That last piece is gold for CRISP-DM: it turns your influence into a documented, auditable process instance.</p>
<h3 data-start="2292" data-end="2358">A practical “options template” you can reuse (work + Module 5)</h3>
<p data-start="2359" data-end="2400">When you present choices, format it like:</p>
<ul data-start="2402" data-end="2736">
<li data-start="2402" data-end="2531">
<p data-start="2404" data-end="2531"><strong data-start="2404" data-end="2442">Option A: Quick insight (2–5 days)</strong><br data-start="2442" data-end="2445">
<em data-start="2447" data-end="2468">Decision supported:</em> …<br data-start="2470" data-end="2473">
<em data-start="2475" data-end="2489">Data needed:</em> …<br data-start="2491" data-end="2494">
<em data-start="2496" data-end="2503">Risk:</em> …<br data-start="2505" data-end="2508">
<em data-start="2510" data-end="2529">Success criteria:</em> …</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2533" data-end="2622">
<p data-start="2535" data-end="2622"><strong data-start="2535" data-end="2576">Option B: Midweight model (2–3 weeks)</strong><br data-start="2576" data-end="2579">
<em data-start="2581" data-end="2602">Decision supported:</em> …<br data-start="2604" data-end="2607">
<em data-start="2609" data-end="2620">Tradeoff:</em> …</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2624" data-end="2736">
<p data-start="2626" data-end="2736"><strong data-start="2626" data-end="2677">Option C: Operationalized solution (4–8+ weeks)</strong><br data-start="2677" data-end="2680">
<em data-start="2682" data-end="2709">Workflow change required:</em> …<br data-start="2711" data-end="2714">
<em data-start="2716" data-end="2734">Monitoring plan:</em> …</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="2738" data-end="2797">Then: <strong data-start="2744" data-end="2797">Recommendation + why + what would change my mind.</strong></p>
<h3 data-start="2799" data-end="2816">The punchline</h3>
<p data-start="2817" data-end="2978">So yeah — analysts often aren’t “leaders” in authority, but they are <strong data-start="2886" data-end="2951">leaders in the way strategy becomes measurable and actionable</strong>. That’s not a small thing.</p>
<p data-start="2980" data-end="3306" data-is-last-node="" data-is-only-node="">If
 you want, give me a real example from your ED world: a typical request 
like “we need data on boarding” / “radiology turnaround is slow” / “LWBS
 is up.” I’ll turn it into a crisp set of options with decision framing +
 success criteria — and it’ll double as a perfect Business Understanding
 artifact for your Module 5 report.</p></div></div></div></div><div class="z-0 flex min-h-[46px] justify-start"><div class="touch:-me-2 touch:-ms-3.5 -ms-2.5 -me-1 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-y-4
