<p data-start="410" data-end="580">I’m giving you <strong data-start="425" data-end="458">copy/paste-ready raw markdown</strong> first (no inline citations inside the block), then a <strong data-start="512" data-end="526">References</strong> section underneath (with sources you can cite later).</p>
<pre class="overflow-visible! px-0!" data-start="582" data-end="13607"><div class="contain-inline-size rounded-2xl corner-superellipse/1.1 relative bg-token-sidebar-surface-primary"><div class="flex items-center text-token-text-secondary px-4 py-2 text-xs font-sans justify-between h-9 bg-token-sidebar-surface-primary select-none rounded-t-2xl corner-t-superellipse/1.1">markdown</div><div class="sticky top-[calc(var(--sticky-padding-top)+9*var(--spacing))]"><div class="absolute end-0 bottom-0 flex h-9 items-center pe-2"><div class="bg-token-bg-elevated-secondary text-token-text-secondary flex items-center gap-4 rounded-sm px-2 font-sans text-xs"><button class="flex gap-1 items-center select-none py-1" aria-label="Copy"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true" class="icon-sm"><use href="/cdn/assets/sprites-core-o8lw6oto.svg#ce3544" fill="currentColor"></use></svg>Copy code</button></div></div></div><div class="overflow-y-auto p-4" dir="ltr"><code class="whitespace-pre! language-markdown"><span><span><span class="hljs-section"># Module 3 — Business Understanding Draft (MIMIC-IV Demo ICU Patient Care Analysis)</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-quote">&gt; <span class="hljs-strong">**AI use note:**</span></span></span><span> This draft was assembled with help from a generative AI assistant acting as a writing/organization aid (summarizing my notes, structuring outlines, and converting brainstormed bullets into a first draft). All project decisions, interpretations, and final wording are mine.

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 1) Background / Context (project framing)</span></span><span>

I am completing a capstone-style case study using the </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**ICU Patient Care Analysis**</span></span><span> option on the </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**MIMIC-IV Clinical Database Demo**</span></span><span> (open-access subset; N≈100 ICU patients). The dataset captures realistic EHR complexity (ICU stays, transfers, vitals, labs, diagnoses, inputs, procedures), but the demo subset is intentionally small and may be sparse for some event tables.

This project is framed with a </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**quality-improvement (QI)-style**</span></span><span> narrative: the goal is to define defensible ICU operational/outcome metrics and explore which </span><span><span class="hljs-emphasis">*patient subgroups and early clinical signals*</span></span><span> are associated with disproportionate resource utilization and worse downstream outcomes (especially </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**hospital readmission**</span></span><span>). The analysis is descriptive and hypothesis-generating (not causal inference).

</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Important dataset constraint:**</span></span><span> dates are </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**patient-shifted**</span></span><span> for de-identification. This preserves within-encounter </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**durations/intervals**</span></span><span> for each patient, but limits cross-patient “true calendar time” analyses (e.g., real-world demand curves by day-of-week across the cohort).  
[Ref A: MIMIC-IV documentation / date shifting]

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Tables already identified as in-scope (current shortlist)</span></span><span>
Hospital / core:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> admissions

ICU / flow:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> icustays
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> transfers

Clinical events:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> labevents + d<span class="hljs-emphasis">_labitems
- chartevents + d_</span>items
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> diagnoses</span><span><span class="hljs-emphasis">_icd + d_</span></span><span>icd<span class="hljs-emphasis">_diagnoses
- inputevents
- procedureevents

### Key outcomes I plan to evaluate (initial shortlist)
- </span></span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**ICU length of stay (ICU LOS):**</span></span><span> ICU admit → ICU discharge (stay-level)
- </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Prolonged ICU stay:**</span></span><span> threshold-based indicator + sensitivity analysis (see Section 6)
- </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Hospital readmission:**</span></span><span> re-hospitalization within a defined window after discharge (see Section 6)
- Optional if feasible (demo-dependent): in-hospital mortality, transfers/ICU returns, procedure-dependent waits

&gt; Note: Early EDA suggests *non-trivial readmission frequency* even with only ~100 patients, making it a viable outcome for subgroup comparisons (with appropriate caution on small N).

---

## 2) Business Objectives &amp; Success Criteria (QI-style)

### 2.1 Primary business objective (decision-support framing)
Identify which ICU patient subgroups and early clinical signals are associated with:
1) </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**disproportionately long ICU stays**</span></span><span> (including “prolonged ICU stay”), and  
2) </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**higher risk of hospital readmission**</span></span><span>,  
in order to generate operationally-relevant hypotheses (e.g., “which cohorts are slower and why”) that an ICU QI team could investigate in a real setting.

This is a demo dataset, so the deliverable is best framed as:
- defensible </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**metric definitions**</span></span><span> + cohort logic,
- clear </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**descriptive findings**</span></span><span> + subgroup comparisons,
- and (if feasible) simple, interpretable </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**predictive prototypes**</span></span><span> using early-window features (no leakage).

### 2.2 Secondary objectives
- </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Define ICU episodes cleanly**</span></span><span> using timestamps and transfers (ICU admit → ICU discharge; handling multiple ICU stays per hospital admission).
- </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Subgroup / pathway analysis:**</span></span><span> test whether outcomes differ across ICU subtypes/cohorts (initial buckets):
  - trauma, neuro, cardiac, sepsis/medical, other
- </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Explain the “why” operationally (hypothesis list):**</span></span><span> for subgroups with longer stays or more readmissions, explore plausible drivers:
  - procedure waits, ventilation/weaning time, lab-dependent delays (e.g., cultures), high measurement intensity as severity proxy, etc.
- </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Validate feasibility:**</span></span><span> quantify missingness/sparsity by table and feature family so the analysis stays honest and right-sized.

### 2.3 Quantitative success criteria (class-appropriate)
- Cohort construction and joins are reproducible and validated at the correct grain (`stay_id</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`, `</span></span><span>hadm</span><span><span class="hljs-emphasis">_id`, `subject_</span></span><span>id`).
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> ICU LOS distributions are summarized overall and by cohort (with uncertainty shown where possible).
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Readmission rate is computed using a documented operational definition (e.g., 30-day) and reported overall + by cohort.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Subgroup comparisons are presented with effect sizes and confidence intervals (not just p-values), with clear caveats about statistical power.

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### 2.4 Qualitative success criteria</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Clear, defensible definitions that avoid incentive-toxic metrics (explicit assumptions and edge cases).
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Transparent discussion of bias risks (measurement intensity, missing-not-at-random, severity confounding).
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> A narrative that would make sense to an ICU leader: what is different across cohorts, what might drive it, and what would be worth investigating operationally.

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 3) Stakeholders + “Decisions this informs” (role-play, demo dataset)</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Primary stakeholder</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**ICU Director**</span></span><span> (most directly accountable for ICU throughput/outcomes and likely to care about prolonged stays and readmissions)

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Secondary stakeholders</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> ICU operations / bed management (capacity, flow)
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Hospital QI leadership (metrics, fairness, definitional defensibility)
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> CMO/executive leadership (high-level outcomes, but less detail than ICU Director)

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Decisions this analysis is meant to inform (tightened)</span></span><span>
1) </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Where to focus QI effort:**</span></span><span> which ICU cohorts show the largest burden of prolonged LOS and/or readmission?
2) </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**What to measure early:**</span></span><span> which </span><span><span class="hljs-emphasis">*early-window*</span></span><span> indicators are feasible and potentially predictive of disproportionate resource use or readmission (without leaking future information)?

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section"># Task 2 — Assess Situation (CRISP-DM)</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 4) Inventory of Resources</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Data resources</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> MIMIC-IV demo tables listed above, plus table dictionaries (</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`d_*`</span></span><span> tables) where available.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> MIMIC documentation for table meanings, key fields, and de-identification constraints.  
[Ref A]

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Compute / workflow resources</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Local repo with version control and a reproducible structure (“show your work”).
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Tooling: pandas-first EDA vs Postgres-first repeatable SQL (decision still open; either is acceptable if documented).

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Domain resources</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> ICU QI framing is based on general operational logic; thresholds/definitions will be supported with literature citations rather than personal opinion.  
[Ref B/C/D]

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 5) Requirements, Assumptions, Constraints</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Requirements</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Reproducible workflow; raw data not committed to Git; clear “how to run” notes.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Explicit definitions for any metric dependent on timestamps, cohort mapping, or windows.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Avoid causal claims; keep inference aligned to what the demo dataset can support.

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Constraints</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Small dataset (N≈100 ICU patients) → limited power for fine-grained subgroup modeling.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> De-identification date shifting → good for within-patient durations; weaker for cross-patient calendar-time utilization claims.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Potential sparsity in event tables (chartevents/labevents/inputevents/procedureevents), varying by patient and cohort.

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Assumptions (explicit)</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Within-patient timestamp ordering is meaningful enough for interval-based features (durations, early windows).
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Cohort grouping using diagnoses (and possibly procedures) is “good enough” for a first-pass pathway model, but must be validated.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Measurement frequency is not random; high measurement can proxy severity and may confound associations.

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 6) Operational Definitions (outcomes + key terms)</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### 6.1 Unit of analysis (candidate)</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Primary: </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**ICU stay**</span></span><span> (</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`stay_id`</span></span><span>) for ICU LOS and early-window features
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Linking: </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**hospital admission**</span></span><span> (</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`hadm_id`</span></span><span>) for readmission logic and discharge timing
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Patient-level: </span><span><span class="hljs-code">`subject_id`</span></span><span> to connect multiple admissions and multiple ICU stays

</span><span><span class="hljs-quote">&gt; [TODO] Finalize which unit drives each section: ICU LOS (stay-level), readmission (admission-level), subgroup (stay-level or admission-level depending on cohort definition).</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### 6.2 Hospital readmission (explicit)</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Hospital readmission**</span></span><span> will be defined as a </span><span><span class="hljs-emphasis">*subsequent hospital admission*</span></span><span> for the same patient (</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`subject_id`</span></span><span>) that occurs within </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**X days**</span></span><span> after discharge of an index admission (</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`hadm_id`</span></span><span>).  
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Default window: </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**30-day readmission**</span></span><span> (common operational standard)  
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Sensitivity: 7/14/30 days if small-N instability suggests it

Implementation approach:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Sort admissions by (</span><span><span class="hljs-code">`subject_id`</span></span><span>, </span><span><span class="hljs-code">`admittime`</span></span><span>)
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> For each index discharge time, flag whether the next </span><span><span class="hljs-code">`admittime`</span></span><span> occurs within the window
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Report overall rate + cohort-stratified rates

[Ref E: readmission within 30 days is a common operational definition; Ref A/F: admissions fields]

</span><span><span class="hljs-quote">&gt; [TODO] Decide whether to exclude planned readmissions (likely not feasible in demo) and how to treat transfers vs true discharge/re-admit.</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### 6.3 Prolonged ICU stay (threshold + sensitivity plan)</span></span><span>
“Prolonged ICU stay” does not have a single universal threshold in the literature; definitions vary by population and study design. The plan is:

</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Primary operational definition (baseline):**</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Prolonged ICU stay = </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**ICU LOS ≥ 14 days**</span></span><span> (initial working threshold)

</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Cohort-aware sensitivity analysis:**</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Trauma/general ICU-like cohorts: test </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**≥ 7 days**</span></span><span> as an alternate threshold
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Neuro/ICH-like cohorts: test </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**≥ 10 days**</span></span><span> as an alternate threshold
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Also test </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**≥ 14 days**</span></span><span> across all cohorts for consistency and comparability

Rationale:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Studies commonly use thresholds in the </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**~7–14 day**</span></span><span> range, and some context-specific definitions use </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**~8 days (trauma)**</span></span><span> or </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**~10 days (ICH)**</span></span><span>.  
[Ref B/C/D]

</span><span><span class="hljs-quote">&gt; [TODO] Add 1–2 strong citations per cohort threshold and decide whether the “main” threshold should be 14 days overall or cohort-specific.  </span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-quote">&gt; [TODO] Decide whether to include a “very long stay” category (e.g., ≥ 21 or ≥ 28 days) if the demo cohort contains outliers.</span></span><span>

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 7) Risks + Contingencies</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Risk: too few cases per subgroup**</span></span><span> → collapse buckets (e.g., neuro vs non-neuro) or focus on descriptive stats only.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Risk: event-table sparsity**</span></span><span> blocks early-window features → fallback to diagnoses/procedures + basic timing features.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Risk: measurement bias**</span></span><span> (sicker patients have more data) → explicitly report measurement counts; use as covariate or caveat.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Risk: leakage**</span></span><span> from late-stay signals → enforce hard early-window cutoff (6h/12h/24h from ICU admit) and document.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Risk: ambiguous readmissions**</span></span><span> (planned vs unplanned) → acknowledge limitation; keep framing as “observed readmission” rather than preventable readmission.

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section"># Task 3 — Determine Data Mining Goals (technical translation)</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 8) Data Mining Goals (draft)</span></span><span>
Given the unit of analysis and definitions above:

1) Build a reliable ICU stay timeline dataset from admissions + icustays + transfers (correct grain; documented joins).  
2) Quantify outcome distributions:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> ICU LOS overall + by cohort
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> prolonged ICU LOS indicator (with sensitivity thresholds)
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> hospital readmission rates (default 30-day) overall + by cohort
3) Prototype </span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**early-window**</span></span><span> features (6/12/24h post-ICU admit) and test whether they are associated with:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> prolonged ICU stay
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> hospital readmission

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">### Data Mining Success Criteria (draft)</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Cohort logic is reproducible and validated.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> Missingness and coverage are summarized for all tables used.
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">-</span></span><span> If modeling is attempted: use simple, interpretable baselines (logistic regression / regularized models), report uncertainty, and treat as exploratory due to N≈100.

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section"># Task 4 — Produce Project Plan (high-level)</span></span><span>

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## 9) Project Plan (draft)</span></span><span>
</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Module 3 (now):**</span></span><span> finalize stakeholders/decisions, operational definitions (readmission + prolonged stay), and assumptions/risks; draft DS goals + plan  
</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Module 4–5:**</span></span><span> data inventory + missingness; finalize cohort buckets; finalize outcome definitions and unit-of-analysis mapping  
</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Module 6–9:**</span></span><span> data prep + descriptive subgroup comparisons; attempt simple early-window models if feasible  
</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Module 10–13:**</span></span><span> evaluation narrative + limitations + “deployment” story (how ICU Director/QI would use this in real practice)  
</span><span><span class="hljs-strong">**Module 14:**</span></span><span> final polish, reflection, and portfolio packaging

---

</span><span><span class="hljs-section">## Notes / What still needs refinement (explicit TODOs)</span></span><span>
1) Confirm readmission window (30-day default) and edge cases:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> planned vs unplanned readmissions (likely not separable)
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> transfers vs discharge/re-admit logic
2) Lock “prolonged ICU stay” threshold strategy:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> single global threshold vs cohort-specific definitions
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> whether to add “very long stay” category
3) Finalize cohort/pathway mapping:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> ICD-only vs ICD + procedure signals
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> how many buckets the demo cohort can support without nonsense comparisons
4) Choose workflow:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> pandas-first vs Postgres-first EDA (either is fine; document rationale)
5) Decide which “why” hypotheses are testable with this demo subset:
</span><span><span class="hljs-bullet">   -</span></span><span> procedure wait proxies, ventilation proxies, culture/lab delay proxies, etc.
</span></span></code></div></div></pre>

class="flex w-full flex-col gap-1 empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="84">Got it — here’s the same content, but more process-diary casual / “future me” voice.</p>
<hr data-start="86" data-end="89">
<p data-start="91" data-end="118"><strong data-start="91" data-end="118">A1. Current Phase Focus</strong></p>
<p data-start="120" data-end="389">This week I’m mostly living in <strong data-start="151" data-end="195">CRISP-DM Phase 1: Business Understanding</strong>.
 I’m basically trying to get the “story + scope + definitions” nailed 
down before I go too deep into data wrangling and accidentally build 
something that doesn’t map cleanly to a real decision.</p>
<p data-start="391" data-end="644">I’ve also been doing a light amount of <strong data-start="430" data-end="461">Phase 2: Data Understanding</strong>
 on the side (mostly sanity checks / feasibility thinking), but the main
 goal right now is to get a workable first draft of the Business 
Understanding section that I can refine later.</p>
<p data-start="646" data-end="688"><strong data-start="646" data-end="688">What I completed in the past two weeks</strong></p>
<ul data-start="690" data-end="2881">
<li data-start="690" data-end="970">
<p data-start="692" data-end="730"><strong data-start="692" data-end="730">Picked the project + got organized</strong></p>
<ul data-start="733" data-end="970">
<li data-start="733" data-end="787">
<p data-start="735" data-end="787">Chose <strong data-start="741" data-end="786">ICU Patient Care Analysis (MIMIC-IV demo)</strong>.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="790" data-end="884">
<p data-start="792" data-end="884">Set up my repo structure so I can “show my work” (notes, process diary, decision log, etc.).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="887" data-end="970">
<p data-start="889" data-end="970">Decided early: <strong data-start="904" data-end="933">raw data stays out of Git</strong> — I’ll document local setup instead.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li data-start="972" data-end="1473">
<p data-start="974" data-end="1012"><strong data-start="974" data-end="1012">Did a quick dataset reconnaissance</strong></p>
<ul data-start="1015" data-end="1473">
<li data-start="1015" data-end="1270">
<p data-start="1017" data-end="1270">Skimmed the MIMIC docs and confirmed which tables I’ll actually need: <code data-start="1087" data-end="1097">patients</code>, <code data-start="1099" data-end="1111">admissions</code>, <code data-start="1113" data-end="1123">icustays</code>, <code data-start="1125" data-end="1136">transfers</code>, plus the big event tables (<code data-start="1165" data-end="1176">labevents</code>, <code data-start="1178" data-end="1191">chartevents</code>, <code data-start="1193" data-end="1208">diagnoses_icd</code>, <code data-start="1210" data-end="1223">inputevents</code>, <code data-start="1225" data-end="1242">procedureevents</code>) and the dictionary tables.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1273" data-end="1473">
<p data-start="1275" data-end="1473">Captured the big dataset constraint: <strong data-start="1312" data-end="1335">MIMIC date shifting</strong> means I can trust <em data-start="1354" data-end="1387">within-stay intervals/durations</em>, but I shouldn’t pretend I can do true calendar-time demand analysis across patients.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li data-start="1475" data-end="2472">
<p data-start="1477" data-end="1553"><strong data-start="1477" data-end="1553">Started writing Business Understanding instead of staring at the ceiling</strong></p>
<ul data-start="1556" data-end="2472">
<li data-start="1556" data-end="1752">
<p data-start="1558" data-end="1752">Committed to a <strong data-start="1573" data-end="1593">QI-style framing</strong>
 (things that resemble real hospital ops analytics: careful metric 
definitions, explicit assumptions, and avoiding misleading 
“single-number” interpretations).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1755" data-end="1953">
<p data-start="1757" data-end="1953">Drafted the Business Understanding 
skeleton: background/context, stakeholders, decision framing, 
assumptions/constraints, risks/contingencies, initial data science 
goals, and a rough project plan.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1956" data-end="2472">
<p data-start="1958" data-end="2034">Logged key decisions (D005–D007) so I don’t keep re-deciding the same stuff:</p>
<ul data-start="2039" data-end="2472">
<li data-start="2039" data-end="2107">
<p data-start="2041" data-end="2107">Stakeholder framing (ICU director / hospital leadership narrative)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2112" data-end="2261">
<p data-start="2114" data-end="2261">Overall approach: break ICU 
patients into subtypes and figure out which groups consume 
disproportionate resources + what early signals predict that</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2266" data-end="2472">
<p data-start="2268" data-end="2472">Early focus ideas: <strong data-start="2287" data-end="2339">readmission seems viable even with ~100 patients</strong>,
 and “prolonged ICU stay” is a real concept but the threshold needs to 
be grounded in the literature (and probably varies by cohort)</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li data-start="2474" data-end="2881">
<p data-start="2476" data-end="2512"><strong data-start="2476" data-end="2512">What I’m still actively deciding</strong></p>
<ul data-start="2515" data-end="2881">
<li data-start="2515" data-end="2625">
<p data-start="2517" data-end="2625">I still need to lock the <strong data-start="2542" data-end="2562">unit of analysis</strong> (<code data-start="2564" data-end="2573">stay_id</code> vs <code data-start="2577" data-end="2586">hadm_id</code> vs <code data-start="2590" data-end="2602">subject_id</code>) based on feasibility.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2628" data-end="2881">
<p data-start="2630" data-end="2881">I also need to finalize the primary endpoint(s) — leaning toward <strong data-start="2695" data-end="2719">hospital readmission</strong> and some definition of <strong data-start="2743" data-end="2764">prolonged ICU LOS</strong>, with thresholds supported by citations (and also sanity-checked against the actual distributions in the demo data).</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<hr data-start="2883" data-end="2887">
<p data-start="2889" data-end="3009">If you want, I can also make an even shorter version (like 6–8 lines) in case the assignment portal is visually hostile.</p>

class="flex w-full flex-col gap-1 empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="267">This week I’m mostly in <strong data-start="24" data-end="69">CRISP-DM Phase 1 (Business Understanding)</strong>.
 I’m trying to get the story, scope, and definitions nailed down before I
 go too deep into data wrangling and accidentally build something that <em data-start="214" data-end="223">doesn’t</em> map cleanly to a real, actionable decision.</p>
<p data-start="269" data-end="840">Over the last two weeks I made the foundational calls: I chose the <strong data-start="336" data-end="381">ICU Patient Care Analysis (MIMIC-IV demo)</strong>
 option, and I set up my Git repo so I can “show my work” in a 
version-controlled, verifiable way (notes, process diary, decision log, 
etc.). I also did a first-pass read through the MIMIC documentation to 
confirm which tables are actually relevant to the kinds of questions I’m
 trying to answer—core tables like admissions/ICU stays/transfers, plus 
the big clinical event tables (labs, charted vitals, diagnoses, inputs, 
procedures) depending on feasibility.</p>
<p data-start="842" data-end="1440">I also used this phase to pressure-test constraints early instead of discovering them later. The big one is the <strong data-start="954" data-end="989">date shifting/de-identification</strong> in MIMIC: it preserves <strong data-start="1013" data-end="1054">within-encounter timing and durations</strong>,
 which is perfect for interval-based metrics, but it limits anything 
that depends on true calendar time across patients (like demand curves 
by day of week). That framing choice pushed me further toward a QI-style
 narrative where I’m explicit about assumptions, careful with 
definitions, and focused on operationally meaningful sub-cycle timelines
 rather than vague one-number outcomes.</p>
<p data-start="1442" data-end="2111">Finally, I started narrowing what 
“success” looks like for this project. The dataset is small (~100 ICU 
patients), so the plan is to keep the analysis defensible: define the 
unit of analysis cleanly, pick outcomes that are actually supported by 
the data, and build a clear translation from stakeholder questions to 
measurable metrics. Early signs from my initial look suggest <strong data-start="1818" data-end="1842">hospital readmission</strong>
 may be viable even with the demo sample size, and I’m also considering a
 “prolonged ICU stay” endpoint—but I need to ground that threshold in 
the literature (since it varies by ICU type/cohort) and then sanity 
check it against the actual distribution in the demo data.</p>
<p data-start="2113" data-end="2313">If you want, I can tighten the last
 paragraph so it reads more like “here’s exactly what I did vs what I’m 
doing next,” but this should be the right tone for a process diary / 
professor-facing answer.</p>
</div></div></div></div><div class="z-0 flex min-h-[46px] justify-start"><div class="touch:-me-2 touch:-ms-3.5 -ms-2.5 -me-1 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-y-4 p-1 select-none I’m trying to lock down the story, scope, and metric definitions <em data-start="136" data-end="144">before</em> I disappear into data wrangling and end up building something that doesn’t map to a real decision.</p>
<p data-start="245" data-end="707">Over the last two weeks I made the foundational moves: I selected the <strong data-start="315" data-end="360">ICU Patient Care Analysis (MIMIC-IV demo)</strong>
 option, and I set up my Git repo so I can “show my work” in a clean, 
version-controlled way (process diary, decision log, notes). I also 
skimmed the MIMIC documentation and confirmed the core tables I’ll 
likely need—admissions/ICU stays/transfers, plus clinical event tables 
(labs, vitals, diagnoses, inputs, procedures) depending on feasibility.</p>
<p data-start="709" data-end="1116">I also used this time to surface constraints early instead of getting surprised later. The big one is MIMIC’s <strong data-start="819" data-end="836">date shifting</strong>:
 it preserves within-encounter durations (which is great for 
interval-based metrics) but limits any analysis that depends on true 
calendar time across patients. That pushed me toward a QI-style framing 
where I’m explicit about assumptions and careful about how I define 
outcomes.</p>
<p data-start="1118" data-end="1448">Next, I’m narrowing the actual endpoints. Early signals from my initial look suggest <strong data-start="1203" data-end="1227">hospital readmission</strong>
 might be feasible even with ~100 patients, and I’m also considering a 
“prolonged ICU stay” outcome—but I’ll need to ground that threshold in 
the literature and then sanity check it against what the demo data can 
support.</p>

empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="266">This week I’m mostly in <strong data-start="24" data-end="69">CRISP-DM Phase 1 (Business Understanding)</strong>. I’m trying to lock down the story, scope, and metric definitions <em data-start="136" data-end="144">before</em> I disappear into data wrangling and accidentally build something that doesn’t map cleanly to a real, actionable decision.</p>
<p data-start="268" data-end="856">Over the last two weeks I knocked out the foundation work: I selected the <strong data-start="342" data-end="387">ICU Patient Care Analysis (MIMIC-IV demo)</strong>
 option, and I set up my Git repo so I can “show my work” in a clean, 
version-controlled way (process diary, decision log, notes, and a 
reproducible folder structure). I also skimmed the MIMIC documentation 
and confirmed the core tables I’ll likely need—<strong data-start="641" data-end="678">admissions / icustays / transfers</strong> for the timeline and flow, plus the event tables (<strong data-start="729" data-end="776">labs, vitals, diagnoses, inputs, procedures</strong>) as optional enrichments depending on how complete they are in the demo subset.</p>
<p data-start="858" data-end="1561">I’ve also been doing quick, targeted
 EDA specifically to surface constraints early instead of getting 
surprised later. The big one is <strong data-start="992" data-end="1017">MIMIC’s date shifting</strong>: it preserves <em data-start="1032" data-end="1050">within-encounter</em> durations (which is perfect for LOS and “time-to-X” style metrics), but it breaks anything that depends on <strong data-start="1158" data-end="1196">true calendar time across patients</strong>.
 So I can’t do the kind of throughput/census-over-time analysis I’m used
 to in an operational setting, because “Jan 10th” in one patient isn’t 
really the same “Jan 10th” in another. That constraint pushed me toward a
 more <strong data-start="1419" data-end="1439">QI-style framing</strong> where I’m explicit about assumptions, careful about leakage, and very precise about how outcomes and windows are defined.</p>
<p data-start="1563" data-end="2308">Next, I’m narrowing the endpoints so the project has a clean spine. Based on what I’ve seen so far, <strong data-start="1663" data-end="1700">hospital readmission / recidivism</strong> looks like it might be feasible even with ~100 patients, and I’m also considering a <strong data-start="1785" data-end="1809">“prolonged ICU stay”</strong>
 outcome. The threshold piece needs a bit of grounding—my working 
intuition is “~14 days” is a common line in the sand, but it varies by 
ICU type and condition—so I’ll do a quick literature pass to pick 
something defensible, then sanity-check it against what the demo data 
can actually support. Overall the dataset is robust in structure, but 
it’s still a smaller and sometimes thinner slice than what I’m used to 
working with day-to-day, so I’m being intentional about scoping to what I
 can defend.</p>
</div></div></div></div><div class="z-0 flex min-h-[46px] justify-start"><div class="touch:-me-2 touch:-ms-3.5 -ms-2.5 -me-1 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-y-4 p-1 select-none <p data-start="157" data-end="764">The main outputs so far are writing + structure: I have a working <strong data-start="223" data-end="255">Business Understanding draft</strong>
 for Module 3 (background, stakeholders, objectives,

 where I’m tracking the big calls (dataset choice, QI-style framing, 
unit-of-analysis still pending EDA, repo hygiene, etc.). I also set up 
the <strong data-start="589" data-end="610">Git repo scaffold</strong> 
so everything is version controlled and easy to audit—notes, drafts, and
 decision history included—so I’m not trying to reconstruct reasoning at
 the end.</p>
<p data-start="766" data-end="1284">On the analysis side, I did some <strong data-start="799" data-end="837">lightweight feasibility/EDA checks</strong>

MIMIC’s <strong data-start="986" data-end="1003">date shifting</strong>

potential endpoints and it looks like <strong data-start="1172" data-end="1196">hospital readmission</strong> may actually be workable even with the small demo cohort, which helps narrow the story.</p>
<p data-start="1286" data-end="1904">All of this connects directly to

inventory/missingness and building the analytic dataset, the report 
already has a stable “spine” (stakeholder decision, unit of analysis, 
outcomes, and success criteria), so the later sections don’t turn into 
last-minute scope chaos.</p>

empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="245">Over the next two weeks I’m planning to shift from “paper decisions” into <strong data-start="74" data-end="96">Data Understanding</strong>,
 but in a controlled way—basically get the dataset into a shape where 
exploration is fast and repeatable without drifting into full-on 
modeling yet.</p>
<p data-start="247" data-end="265">My main goals are:</p>
<ul data-start="267" data-end="1145">
<li data-start="267" data-end="513">
<p data-start="269" data-end="513"><strong data-start="269" data-end="333">Load the MIMIC-IV demo tables into a local Postgres database</strong>
 so I can explore with SQL instead of doing everything in pandas. For me
 that’s the difference between poking at data and actually being able to
 iterate quickly and stay organized.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="514" data-end="837">
<p data-start="516" data-end="589">Do a focused <strong data-start="529" data-end="566">data inventory / feasibility pass</strong> once it’s in Postgres:</p>
<ul data-start="592" data-end="837">
<li data-start="592" data-end="667">
<p data-start="594" data-end="667">confirm row counts at the key grains (<code data-start="632" data-end="644">subject_id</code>, <code data-start="646" data-end="655">hadm_id</code>, <code data-start="657" data-end="666">stay_id</code>)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="670" data-end="737">
<p data-start="672" data-end="737">confirm join paths (patients → admissions → icustays → transfers)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="740" data-end="837">
<p data-start="742" data-end="837">quick missingness / coverage checks for the big event tables (labs, vitals, inputs, procedures)</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li data-start="838" data-end="1145">
<p data-start="840" data-end="914">Based on that, <strong data-start="855" data-end="890">commit the core scope decisions</strong> I’ve been holding open:</p>
<ul data-start="917" data-end="1145">
<li data-start="917" data-end="945">
<p data-start="919" data-end="945">final <strong data-start="925" data-end="945">unit of analysis</strong></p>
</li>
<li data-start="948" data-end="1049">
<p data-start="950" data-end="1049">primary endpoint(s) (likely readmission + maybe prolonged ICU stay if the distribution supports it)</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1052" data-end="1145">
<p data-start="1054" data-end="1145">pick an “early window” definition that avoids leakage and is supported by timestamp density</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="1147" data-end="1625">In terms of milestones: my personal deadline is to have the <strong data-start="1207" data-end="1274">Postgres load + basic table inventory done within the next week</strong>,
 because once that’s working I can move much faster. Then by the end of 
the two weeks I want to have a “minimum viable” Data Understanding 
snapshot—basically enough concrete evidence (counts, missingness, 
feasibility notes) that I can confidently lock the endpoints and start 
drafting the Data Understanding section for Assignment 1 without 
guessing.</p>

<p data-start="148" data-end="515">One of my main short-term goals going
 forward is getting the MIMIC-IV demo tables loaded into a local 
Postgres database so I can explore with SQL instead of doing everything 
in pandas. For this kind of project, SQL makes iteration faster and 
keeps me more organized—especially when I’m trying to sanity-check 
joins, grains, and timestamp logic across multiple tables.</p>
<p data-start="517" data-end="1032">Once that’s in place, I want to do a
 more focused feasibility pass: confirm row counts at the 
patient/admission/ICU-stay levels, validate the join paths (patients → 
admissions → icustays → transfers), and get a quick read on 
coverage/missingness for the main event tables (labs, vitals, inputs, 
procedures). I also need to generate an ER diagram I can refer to as a 
“source of truth” while I’m writing and while I’m building the analytic 
dataset, so I’m not relying on memory or constantly re-reading 
documentation.</p>
<p data-start="1034" data-end="1100">If you want it slightly more casual / professor-conversation tone:</p>
<p data-start="1102" data-end="1576">A big near-term goal is to load the
 tables into local Postgres so I can work in SQL instead of living in 
pandas. That’ll make it way easier to iterate and to keep my joins 
straight. Once that’s set up, I’m going to do a tighter feasibility 
check—counts by patient/admission/stay, confirm the join routes, and see
 how complete the key event tables are. I also need to build an ER 
diagram so I have a consistent map of the schema as I move into the Data
 Understanding section.</p>
<p data-start="1578" data-end="1684">Want me to blend this directly into your full A3 answer so it flows with what you already wrote for A1/A2?</p>

<h3 data-start="138" data-end="177">Option A (straightforward + honest)</h3>
<p data-start="178" data-end="710">For this project specifically, I 
haven’t really learned brand-new technical skills yet—I’ve mostly been 
applying things I already do at work (keeping a clean repo, documenting 
decisions, and setting up a workflow that’s reproducible). What <em data-start="418" data-end="423">has</em>
 been new and genuinely helpful is the MIMIC documentation and data 
dictionary on the MIMIC site. It’s the difference between guessing what a
 field means vs actually understanding the intent of the table design 
and the joins, especially with ICU stays/transfers and all the event 
tables.</p>
<p data-start="712" data-end="1248">From the course materials, the most 
useful piece so far was honestly the “cookie cutter” call-out earlier in
 the module—basically the idea of using a repeatable template to spin up
 a consistent directory structure and documentation habits <em data-start="951" data-end="959">before</em>
 you start coding. I already do a version of that in real projects, but 
having it framed as a deliberate “tool I didn’t know I needed” was a 
great reminder. It makes it way easier to move fast without creating 
chaos, and it’s already paying off as I build the Business Understanding
 draft.</p>
<h3 data-start="1250" data-end="1303">Option B (a little more personality / reflective)</h3>
<p data-start="1304" data-end="1719">I haven’t picked up new tools or 
fancy techniques for this project yet—so far it’s been more about 
applying good habits on purpose instead of stumbling into them. The most
 helpful “technical” learning has actually been the MIMIC data 
dictionary and documentation. It’s forcing me to stay disciplined about 
definitions and grain (patient vs admission vs ICU stay) instead of 
hand-waving and then paying for it later.</p>
<p data-start="1721" data-end="2162">On the course side, the thing that 
stuck with me was the cookie-cutter idea from the earlier module. I 
already use directory structure patterns at work, but the way it was 
presented—as a repeatable template you can stamp out quickly—was weirdly
 satisfying. It’s a small piece of “tech,” but it prevents a ton of 
friction later. It also fits perfectly with the CRISP-DM mindset: get 
organized early so you can iterate without losing the plot.</p>
<p data-start="2164" data-end="2281">If you want, tell me which tone you like (A vs B), and I’ll tighten it further to match the rest of your diary voice.</p>

empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="192">Here’s
 a tightened, narrative-style draft that keeps your voice and hits both 
prompts (real-world relevance + professional skills), with a light nod 
to the politics piece without derailing it:</p>
<p data-start="194" data-end="834">I actually have a bit of a unique 
lens on this because I do this for real in my day job as a BI Specialist
 III at UCI Health. The way the course frames CRISP-DM—starting with 
business understanding, forcing clear definitions, documenting 
assumptions, and tying analysis to an actual decision—is <em data-start="489" data-end="495">very</em>
 close to what I see in operational healthcare analytics. In that sense,
 this project doesn’t feel like a classroom toy problem. It feels like a
 respectable “mini version” of the kind of work I’d get pulled into when
 leadership is asking, “Where are we getting stuck, which patients are 
driving it, and what levers do we actually control?”</p>
<p data-start="836" data-end="1467">The main difference in the real 
world is that analytics never lives in a vacuum. Even when the numbers 
are correct, how you frame them matters because incentives and politics 
are always in the room—especially in a hospital. A metric can be 
technically valid but still land wrong if it implies blame, threatens 
budgets, or gets interpreted as “your department is the problem.” The 
course doesn’t lean hard into that aspect (which is understandable), but
 it’s something I’m keeping in mind as I write: be explicit about 
assumptions, define metrics carefully, and avoid conclusions that imply 
causality when the data can’t support it.</p>
<p data-start="1469" data-end="1949">Beyond the technical work, I’m 
developing professional skills that translate directly to practice: 
scoping a project so it’s actually finishable, writing definitions that 
other people can audit, keeping a clean decision log so I can justify 
choices later, and building a reproducible workflow that makes the 
analysis defensible. Honestly, that combination—clear communication + 
disciplined scope + documentation—is what makes analytics usable in real
 settings, not just “correct.”</p>
<p data-start="1951" data-end="2077">If you want it <em data-start="1966" data-end="1976">slightly</em> more casual (or slightly more “professor-friendly”), tell me which direction and I’ll tune the tone.</p>

empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="132">Here’s
 a draft in the same “talking to the prof” style—casual, specific, and 
honest—without sounding like you’re stuck in the weeds:</p>
<p data-start="134" data-end="607">Right now my main challenge is less 
“can I do the analysis?” and more “how do I make the scope defensible 
with the demo constraints.” The MIMIC demo dataset is small enough that 
missingness and sparsity aren’t just annoying—they can completely 
determine what questions are even answerable. So I’m trying to avoid 
falling into the trap of writing an ambitious business story and then 
discovering the event tables don’t actually support the feature set or 
timelines I’d need.</p>
<p data-start="609" data-end="661">Concretely, I’m wrestling with three related things:</p>
<ol data-start="663" data-end="1938">
<li data-start="663" data-end="1155">
<p data-start="666" data-end="1155"><strong data-start="666" data-end="704">Outcome definition vs feasibility.</strong>
 I’m leaning toward hospital readmission because it looks like there’s 
enough signal even with ~100 patients, and I’m also considering 
“prolonged ICU stay.” But “prolonged” has real clinical definitions that
 vary by ICU type, so I need to pick a threshold that’s both 
literature-backed <em data-start="990" data-end="995">and</em> actually 
results in enough cases in this cohort to analyze. If I pick something 
too strict, I end up with a handful of positives and the whole thing 
collapses.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1157" data-end="1569">
<p data-start="1160" data-end="1569"><strong data-start="1160" data-end="1204">Cohort grouping without over-segmenting.</strong>
 Breaking ICU stays into trauma/neuro/cardiac/sepsis/etc. makes the 
story make sense, but with a small N it’s easy to create tiny buckets 
that don’t support comparisons. I need a grouping scheme that’s 
clinically coherent <em data-start="1426" data-end="1431">and</em> 
statistically survivable. That’s partly conceptual (how to define the 
cohorts) and partly process (knowing when to simplify and move on).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1571" data-end="1938">
<p data-start="1574" data-end="1938"><strong data-start="1574" data-end="1632">Avoiding leakage while still having enough early data.</strong>
 I want to engineer early-window features (6–24 hours from ICU 
admission), but depending on how dense the vitals/labs are in the demo 
subset, a strict early window might wipe out a lot of usable features. 
So I’m trying to balance “clean methodology” with “do I actually have 
enough data to build anything.”</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p data-start="1940" data-end="2305">So it’s a mix of conceptual and 
process challenges: making the project tight enough to be defensible, 
but still interesting and rich enough to be worth doing. My plan to 
break the logjam is to do a focused feasibility pass (coverage, 
missingness, counts per cohort/outcome) and then lock the endpoints and 
cohort buckets based on what the data can actually support.</p>
<p data-start="2307" data-end="2532">If you want, I can make this even 
more “example-style” by adding one concrete number you’ve seen so far 
(e.g., “readmission appears in X out of ~100”)—but I kept it general 
since you haven’t dropped the exact counts here yet.</p>

empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="365">Right
 now my main challenge is scoping the project in a way that’s both 
defensible and feasible with the MIMIC demo constraints. With only ~100 
patients, missingness and sparsity are not just inconvenient. They can 
completely determine what questions are answerable, so I’m trying to 
avoid writing an ambitious story and then discovering the data cannot 
support it.</p>
<p data-start="367" data-end="794">The biggest sticking points are 
outcome and cohort definitions. I’m leaning toward hospital readmission 
because it looks like there’s enough signal even at this size, and I’m 
also considering a “prolonged ICU stay” outcome. The problem is that 
“prolonged” has real clinical thresholds that vary by ICU type, so I 
need a definition that I can justify with literature and that still 
yields enough cases in this cohort to analyze.</p>
<p data-start="796" data-end="1156">I’m also trying to group ICU 
patients into clinically meaningful buckets like trauma, neuro, cardiac,
 sepsis, etc., without over-segmenting into tiny groups that make 
comparisons meaningless. Finally, I want to engineer early-window 
features (first 6 to 24 hours) without leakage, but that depends on how 
dense the early labs and vitals are in the demo tables.</p>
<p data-start="1158" data-end="1362">So it’s a mix of conceptual and 
process issues. My plan is to do a focused feasibility pass on coverage 
and counts, then lock the outcomes and cohort structure based on what 
the data can actually support.</p>

<p data-start="637" data-end="951">On the technical side, I’d like more

validating that the features truly come from the intended time slice.</p>

heuristics for choosing the right unit of analysis (patient vs admission
 vs ICU stay) when the tables naturally live at different grains. I know

what to do when the “right” grain depends on missingness and what 
outcomes are actually feasible.</p>

wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="118">I’m mostly feeling solid on the overall direction, but I do have a few gaps I want to tighten up before I go too deep.</p>
<p data-start="120" data-end="458">The biggest one is having a concrete,
 defensible method for locking an outcome definition when the dataset is
 small. For example, “prolonged ICU stay” needs to be grounded in 
literature and then sanity-checked against what the demo cohort can 
actually support, so I’m not picking a cutoff that’s either arbitrary or
 statistically useless.</p>
<p data-start="460" data-end="512">The other things I still want to get sharper on are:</p>
<ul data-start="514" data-end="1360">
<li data-start="514" data-end="692">
<p data-start="516" data-end="692">How to choose the right grain 
(patient vs admission vs ICU stay) in a way that matches the question, 
avoids double counting, and still gives me enough sample size to work 
with.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="693" data-end="836">
<p data-start="695" data-end="836">How to define readmission cleanly in 
this dataset (what counts as a readmission, what time window makes 
sense, and how to handle edge cases).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="837" data-end="1003">
<p data-start="839" data-end="1003">How to engineer early-window 
features without leakage in a way that’s consistent and auditable, 
especially when the early labs and vitals might be sparse or uneven.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1004" data-end="1154">
<p data-start="1006" data-end="1154">How to deal with missingness and 
measurement bias in ICU data, where sicker patients get measured more 
and “missing” can actually mean “doing fine.”</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1155" data-end="1360">
<p data-start="1157" data-end="1360">What “right-sized” model evaluation
 looks like for N around 100 so I don’t pretend I can prove more than I 
can, but still do something rigorous (baselines, simple validation 
strategy, clear uncertainty).</p>
</li>
</ul>

empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="583">I
 haven’t learned a brand-new modeling technique for this project yet. So
 far it’s been more about setting the foundation correctly. The main 
“new learning” for me has actually been Cookiecutter (the open-source 
project templating tool mentioned in an earlier module). I’d never used 
it before this class, and it’s honestly been one of the most immediately
 useful takeaways. I’ve already started using it at work to initialize 
projects with a consistent structure (folders, README scaffolding, 
configs, etc.), which saves time and is already preventing the usual 
early-project chaos.</p>
<p data-start="585" data-end="945">What’s interesting is how that 
connects to a bigger pattern that shows up across a lot of different 
areas of data science: most of the leverage isn’t in the fancy model, 
it’s in making the work reproducible, auditable, and easy to iterate on.
 Whether you’re doing forecasting, clinical analytics, NLP, or 
causal-ish evaluation, the same themes keep showing up:</p>
<ul data-start="947" data-end="2281">
<li data-start="947" data-end="1152">
<p data-start="949" data-end="1152"><strong data-start="949" data-end="991">Reproducibility is a force multiplier.</strong>
 A clean repo structure, clear configs, and a “show your work” trail 
matters in every domain. You can’t debug, validate, or hand off work if 
it’s not repeatable.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1154" data-end="1467">
<p data-start="1156" data-end="1467"><strong data-start="1156" data-end="1188">Definitions beat algorithms.</strong>
 The hard part across projects is usually locking down what the target 
actually means (readmission, prolonged stay, churn, “failure,” etc.). 
That’s true in healthcare, finance, marketing, and ops analytics. If the
 outcome definition is shaky, the model is just confidently wrong.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1469" data-end="1790">
<p data-start="1471" data-end="1790"><strong data-start="1471" data-end="1532">Data quality and measurement bias are universal problems.</strong>
 ICU data has “sicker patients get measured more,” but retail has 
“high-value customers generate more signal,” and product analytics has 
“power users create more events.” Different domains, same issue: 
missingness isn’t random and you have to account for it.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1792" data-end="2019">
<p data-start="1794" data-end="2019"><strong data-start="1794" data-end="1836">Iteration loops are the real workflow.</strong>
 CRISP-DM isn’t just a classroom framework. In practice, you keep 
bouncing between business understanding, data understanding, and 
preparation as soon as reality shows up in the data.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="2021" data-end="2281">
<p data-start="2023" data-end="2281"><strong data-start="2023" data-end="2097">Communication and stakeholder alignment is part of the technical work.</strong>
 Even when you’re not “deploying” anything, you’re always translating 
between what the data can support and what someone wants the answer to 
be. That applies across every flavor of DS.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="2283" data-end="2550">So even though I haven’t learned a new modeling trick yet, I <em data-start="2344" data-end="2350">have</em>
 been reinforcing the cross-cutting habits that make any DS project 
actually succeed: structured workflow, explicit assumptions, defensible 
metrics, and the ability to iterate without losing the plot.</p>
</div></div></div></div><div class="z-0 flex min-h-[46px] justify-start"><div class="touch:-me-2 touch:-ms-3.5 -ms-2.5 -me-1 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-y-4 p-1 select-none empty:hidden first:pt-[1px]"><div class="markdown prose dark:prose-invert w-full wrap-break-word dark markdown-new-styling"><p data-start="0" data-end="116">You can keep it simple and honest, but still give them <em data-start="55" data-end="77">something actionable</em> so it doesn’t read like “no feedback.”</p>
<p data-start="118" data-end="175">Here are 3 options (pick the one that matches your vibe):</p>
<p data-start="177" data-end="511"><strong data-start="177" data-end="217">Option A (straightforward, minimal):</strong><br data-start="217" data-end="220">
Right now I’m doing fine working independently. If I hit a blocker, I’ll
 either email the teaching team or hop into office hours. The main thing
 that would help is quick feedback if I’m about to lock in a shaky 
outcome definition, since small datasets don’t leave much room to 
recover later.</p>
<p data-start="513" data-end="883"><strong data-start="513" data-end="559">Option B (a little warmer, still concise):</strong><br data-start="559" data-end="562">
I’m in a good spot and don’t need much hands-on support at the moment. 
If something comes up, I’ll use office hours or email. If you had one 
“sanity check” resource to point to, it would be guidance on defining 
defensible outcomes and thresholds with small N, especially for things 
like prolonged ICU stay or readmission.</p>
<p data-start="885" data-end="1192"><strong data-start="885" data-end="923">Option C (super casual, very you):</strong><br data-start="923" data-end="926">
I’m good for now and I’m comfortable working solo. If I get stuck, I’ll 
just email or jump on office hours. The only thing I might want a quick 
gut check on later is whether my outcome definitions are defensible 
given the demo dataset size, before I commit too hard.</p>
<p data-start="1194" data-end="1338">If you want my recommendation: go with <strong data-start="1233" data-end="1245">Option A</strong>. It says “I’m fine,” but also signals you’re thinking like a grown-up about avoiding rework.</p>

Copy/paste as-is:</p>
<p data-start="160" data-end="715">I just want to say the way this 
course frames the work through CRISP-DM feels surprisingly close to real
 analytics practice, at least in healthcare ops and QI. The repeated 
emphasis on translating messy organizational questions into clean 
definitions, documenting assumptions, and being explicit about what the 
data can and cannot support is exactly the part that usually gets 
skipped in the real world and then causes problems later. I also 
appreciate that the assignments reward “showing your work” and decision 
traceability, not just producing a model.</p>
<p data-start="717" data-end="1182">One thing I’ve found especially 
valuable is how much the course pushes structure early. I tend to be 
very self-directed and can go deep fast, but the process diary + 
decision log approach is helping me slow down in a productive way and 
lock scope before I overbuild. Cookiecutter was also a genuinely useful 
surprise. I’d never used it before, and I’ve already started applying it
 at work to standardize project scaffolding and reduce the usual 
early-project chaos.</p>
<p data-start="1184" data-end="1676">If I had one small suggestion, it 
would be a little more concrete guidance on defensible outcome 
definitions when working with small datasets like the MIMIC demo. In 
real settings, you can usually solve that with volume or stakeholder 
iteration, but in a course setting you sometimes have to “pick a 
definition and live with it,” so having a short rubric or a couple 
healthcare examples (prolonged ICU stay thresholds, readmission windows,
 etc.) would make that step feel less like guesswork.</p>
<p data-start="1678" data-end="1813">Overall though, this is a solid and
 respectable setup, and I’m getting real-world value out of it, not just
 checking a box for a grade.</p>

 it. Here’s a version that keeps your point, but frames it in a way

 course to become a political science class.</p>
<p data-start="189" data-end="231">You can paste this as your updated <strong data-start="224" data-end="230">C4</strong>:</p>
<p data-start="233" data-end="456">I’ve really liked how close the 
CRISP-DM framing is to real analytics work, especially the emphasis on 
defining metrics carefully, documenting assumptions, and avoiding 
“analysis theater.” That part feels very true to life.</p>
<p data-start="458" data-end="1163">The only gap I keep noticing is the 
political layer that comes with executive-facing analytics. In real 
hospital ops work, the same numbers can land very differently depending 
on incentives, who owns the metric, and what story leadership is trying 
to support. To be clear, I don’t expect this course to turn into org 
politics training, and in practice there’s usually leadership above you 
that understands that layer and helps navigate it. But even a short 
callout on “how to communicate results safely” would be useful, like 
examples of wording that avoids blame, how to separate what a department
 controls versus what it doesn’t, and how to frame limitations without 
sounding like you’re making excuses.</p>
<p data-start="1165" data-end="1245">Overall, the course structure is solid and I’m getting real-world value from it.</p>

theater” is when the work <em data-start="36" data-end="43">looks</em>
 rigorous and data-driven, but it’s mostly performance — the analysis is
 optimized for optics, storytelling, or checking a box, not for actually
 improving a decision.</p>
<p data-start="211" data-end="266">A few concrete examples (especially in ops/healthcare):</p>
<ul data-start="268" data-end="1399">
<li data-start="268" data-end="442">
<p data-start="270" data-end="442"><strong data-start="270" data-end="315">Pretty dashboards with shaky definitions.</strong> Everyone debates colors and layout, but nobody can explain how “LOS” is defined, what timestamps are used, or what’s excluded.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="443" data-end="630">
<p data-start="445" data-end="630"><strong data-start="445" data-end="464">Vanity metrics.</strong>
 Tracking something because it’s easy to measure or makes leadership 
feel in control, even if it doesn’t map to an actionable lever (or it 
incentivizes bad behavior).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="631" data-end="797">
<p data-start="633" data-end="797"><strong data-start="633" data-end="653">False precision.</strong>
 Reporting numbers to two decimals and fancy trend lines when the 
underlying data quality/missingness makes that level of certainty 
meaningless.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="798" data-end="940">
<p data-start="800" data-end="940"><strong data-start="800" data-end="842">Model-first instead of decision-first.</strong> Building a model because it’s cool, then trying to retrofit a “business question” after the fact.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="941" data-end="1073">
<p data-start="943" data-end="1073"><strong data-start="943" data-end="965">Selective slicing.</strong> Choosing subgroup cuts that “support” a narrative rather than ones that are defensible, stable, and useful.</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1074" data-end="1259">
<p data-start="1076" data-end="1259"><strong data-start="1076" data-end="1109">Ignoring assumptions/leakage.</strong>
 The analysis “wins” on paper, but only because it accidentally used 
information that wouldn’t exist at decision time (common in clinical 
event data).</p>
</li>
<li data-start="1260" data-end="1399">
<p data-start="1262" data-end="1399"><strong data-start="1262" data-end="1286">No operational plan.</strong> Great findings, zero pathway to adoption: no owners, no measurement plan, no monitoring, no changes to workflow.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p data-start="1401" data-end="1602">In contrast, what you’re doing (and
 what CRISP-DM pushes) is the antidote: lock definitions, document 
assumptions, align metrics to decisions, and be explicit about what the 
data can and can’t support.</p>
<p data-start="1604" data-end="1704">If you want, I can rewrite that C4 paragraph to avoid the phrase entirely while keeping the meaning.</p>

The only gap I've noticed is the political layer that comes with executive-facing analytics. In real hospital ops work, the same numbers can land very differently depending on incentives, who owns the metric, and what story leadership is trying to support. To be clear, I don’t expect this course to turn into org politics training, and in practice there’s usually leadership above you that understands that layer and helps navigate it. But even a short callout on “how to communicate results safely” would probably be useful, like examples of wording that avoids blame, or how to separate what a department controls versus what it doesn’t, and how to frame limitations without sounding like you’re making excuses.</div></div></div></div></div></div></div><span class="sr-only"><br></span></article><article class="text-token-text-primary w-full focus:outline-none [--shadow-height:45px] has-data-writing-block:pointer-events-none has-data-writing-block:-mt-(--shadow-height) has-data-writing-block:pt-(--shadow-height) [&amp;:has([data-writing-block])&gt;*]:pointer-events-auto scroll-mt-(--header-height)" tabindex="-1" dir="auto" data-turn-id="45aabaa6-81ef-479b-8684-fa7f0618bf12" data-testid="conversation-turn-175" data-scroll-anchor="false" data-turn="user"><h5 class="sr-only">You said:</h5><div class="text-base my-auto mx-auto [--thread-content-margin:--spacing(4)] @w-sm/main:[--thread-content-margin:--spacing(6)] @w-lg/main:[--thread-content-margin:--spacing(16)] px-(--thread-content-margin)"><div class="[--thread-content-max-width:40rem] @w-lg/main:[--thread-content-max-width:48rem] mx-auto max-w-(--thread-content-max-width) flex-1 group/turn-messages focus-visible:outline-hidden relative flex w-full min-w-0 flex-col" tabindex="-1"><div class="flex max-w-full flex-col grow"><div data-message-author-role="user" data-message-id="45aabaa6-81ef-479b-8684-fa7f0618bf12" dir="auto" class="min-h-8 text-message relative flex w-full flex-col items-end gap-2 text-start break-words whitespace-normal [.text-message+&amp;]:mt-1"><div class="flex w-full flex-col gap-1 empty:hidden items-end rtl:items-start"><div class="user-message-bubble-color corner-superellipse/1.1 relative rounded-[18px] px-4 py-1.5 data-[multiline]:py-3 max-w-[var(--user-chat-width,70%)]" data-multiline=""><div class="whitespace-pre-wrap">this is what I submitted... """The Process Diary is a formative assessment designed to help you reflect on your project progress, connect new learning to previous knowledge, and identify areas where you need support. This is a graded activity that provides valuable feedback to both you and the teaching team about your learning journey.

Format: Short written responses (approximately 500-750 words total) 
Submission Guidelines

    Length: Aim for 500-750 words total across all sections

    Tone: Honest and reflective - this is for your learning benefit

    Specificity: Use concrete examples rather than general statements

    For full points, you must answer all questions; if the question does not apply please type "N/A" or "not applicable."

Example Response (Partial)

A1. Current Phase Focus I'm primarily working on the Data Understanding phase, specifically exploring the customer transaction dataset for my retail analytics project. This week I’m mostly in CRISP-DM Phase 1 (Business Understanding). I’m trying to lock down the story, scope, and metric definitions before I dive too deep into data wrangling and accidentally build something that would not map cleanly to a real, actionable decision. Over the last two weeks I knocked out the foundation work: I selected the ICU Patient Care Analysis (MIMIC-IV demo) option, and I set up my Git repo so I can “show my work” in a clean, version-controlled way (process diary, decision log, notes, and a reproducible folder structure). I also skimmed the MIMIC documentation and confirmed the core tables I’ll likely need—admissions / icustays / transfers for the timeline and flow, plus the event tables (labs, vitals, diagnoses, inputs, procedures) as possible featutres depending on how complete they are in the demo subset and how strong predictors they are. I’ve also been doing quick, targeted EDA specifically to surface any constraints early instead of getting a surprised later. The big one is MIMIC’s date shifting: it preserves within-encounter durations (which is perfect for LOS and “time-to-X” style metrics), but it breaks anything that depends on true calendar time across patients. So I can’t do the kind of throughput/census-over-time analysis I’m used to in an operational setting, because “Jan 10th” in one patient isn’t really the same “Jan 10th” in another. That constraint is pushing me toward a more QI-style framing where I’m explicit about assumptions and very precise about how outcomes and windows are defined. Next, I’m narrowing the endpoints so the project has a clean spine. Based on what I’ve seen so far, hospital readmission / recidivism looks like it might be feasible even with ~100 patients, and I’m also considering a “prolonged ICU stay” outcome. The threshold piece needs a bit of grounding...my working intuition is “~14 days” is a common line in the sand (at least in ops projects ive been involved in), but it varies by ICU type and condition...so I’ll do a quick literature pass to pick something defensible, then sanity-check it against what the demo data can actually support. Overall the dataset is robust in structure, but it’s still a smaller and sometimes thinner slice than what I’m used to working with day-to-day, so I’m being intentional about scoping to what I can defend.
1 / 1 point

I actually have a bit of a unique lens on this because I do this for real in my day job as a BI Specialist III at UCI Health. The way the course frames CRISP-DM...starting with business understanding, forcing clear definitions, documenting assumptions, and tying analysis to an actual decision...is very close to what I see in operational healthcare analytics. In that sense, this project doesn’t feel like a classroom toy problem. It feels like a respectable “mini version” of the kind of work I’d get pulled into when leadership is asking, “Where are we getting stuck, which patients are driving it, and what levers do we actually control?” The main difference in the real world is that analytics never lives in a vacuum. Even when the numbers are correct, how you frame them matters because incentives and politics are always in the room. Especially in a hospital. A metric can be technically valid but still land wrong if it implies blame, threatens budgets, or gets interpreted as “your department is the problem.” The course doesn’t lean hard into that aspect (which is understandable), but it’s something I’m keeping in mind as I write: be explicit about assumptions, define metrics carefully, and avoid conclusions that imply causality when the data can’t support it. But Beyond the technical work, I’m developing professional skills that translate directly to practice: scoping a project so it’s actually finishable, writing definitions that other people can audit, keeping a clean decision log so I can justify choices later, and building a reproducible workflow that makes the analysis defensible.
1 / 1 point

Right now my main challenge is scoping the project in a way that’s defensible and feasible with the MIMIC demo constraints and generates actionable insights I would be happy to present to a CMO or ICU Director. But with only ~100 patients, missingness and sparsity are not just inconvenient.... they can completely determine what questions that are answerable, so I’m trying to avoid writing an overly ambitious story and then discovering the data cannot support it. The biggest sticking points are outcome and cohort definitions. I’m leaning toward hospital readmission because it looks like there’s enough signal even at this size, and I’m also considering a “prolonged ICU stay” outcome. The problem is that “prolonged” has real clinical thresholds that vary by ICU type, so I need a definition that I can justify with literature and that still yields enough cases in this cohort to analyze. I’m also trying to group ICU patients into clinically meaningful buckets like trauma, neuro, cardiac, sepsis, etc., without over-segmenting into tiny groups that make comparisons meaningless. Finally, I want to build predictors using only information we’d realistically have early in the ICU stay (like the first 6–24 hours), so I’m not accidentally “cheating” by using data that only shows up later. But whether I can do that depends on whether the dataset actually has enough labs and vitals recorded during that early window for most patients. If early measurements are sparse or missing for a lot of people, those early predictors won’t be reliable. So it’s a mix of conceptual and process issues. My plan is to do a focused feasibility pass on coverage and counts, then lock the outcomes and cohort structure based on what the data can actually support.

I’ve really liked how close the CRISP-DM framing is to real analytics work, especially the emphasis on defining metrics carefully, documenting assumptions, and avoiding “analysis theater” where the work just looks rigorous and data-driven but is mostly optimized for performative optics, not actually improving a decision. That part feels very true to life. I’ve seen organizations spend millions on big-name consultants from places like McKinsey &amp; Company or Accenture just to rubber-stamp a direction leadership already wanted, even when the underlying logic is shaky. This course structure feels like it pushes the opposite muscle: slow down, make the definitions defensible, and make sure the analysis actually connects to an actionable lever. The only gap I've noticed is the political layer that comes with executive-facing analytics. In real hospital ops work, the same numbers can land very differently depending on incentives, who owns the metric, and what story leadership is trying to support. To be clear, I don’t expect this course to turn into org politics training, and in practice there’s usually leadership above you that understands that layer and helps navigate it. But even a short callout on “how to communicate results safely” would probably be useful, like examples of wording that avoids blame, or how to separate what a department controls versus what it doesn’t, and how to frame limitations without sounding like you’re making excuses.
1 / 1 point
